Men who have sex with men with high-risk behavior: ask an HIV-designated hospital about PrEP — taken on schedule it cuts infections by 70%+

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: highTime: mediumWillpower: someBenefit: large

People not yet infected can take an antiviral in advance — pre-exposure prophylaxis. Taken on schedule, infection risk drops by 70% or more. Taken on and off, it does essentially nothing. It's prescription-only: you get tested first, then it's prescribed, then periodic follow-up.

Cost
This is prescription medication, self-paid in most places, from a few hundred to a few thousand yuan. Before starting: HIV, kidney function, and hepatitis B tests. Then follow-up every 3 months. The hard part is taking it daily, on schedule.
Benefit
The drug is a combination of emtricitabine and tenofovir. The iPrEx trial had 2,499 men who have sex with men and transgender women take the pill daily or placebo. The drug group had 44% fewer infections (95% CI 15–63). Among those with detectable drug in their blood, protection was far stronger. The UK PROUD trial enrolled 544 gay and bisexual men: those starting immediately had 86% fewer infections than those deferred a year (90% CI 64–96 — a 90% confidence range). France's IPERGAY trial used on-demand dosing before and after sex: 86% fewer infections (95% CI 40–98). A meta-analysis WHO relies on pooled the trials: overall RR 0.49 (0.33–0.73, about 51% lower). In trials where more than 70% of doses were taken as scheduled, RR 0.30 (0.21–0.45, about 70% lower). Where adherence was under 40%, RR 0.95 — essentially no effect. China's NMPA approved the drug for pre-exposure prophylaxis in August 2020, for adults and adolescents weighing at least 35 kg (multinational / China)
Note
Trial populations were mostly men who have sex with men, so they're the ones who should ask. Others with high-risk sex can ask a doctor whether it suits them. Before prescribing, absence of infection must be confirmed — taking it while already infected breeds resistant virus, and a self-test strip doesn't count as the basis. People with hepatitis B can flare when stopping, hence the pre-prescription test. WHO endorses on-demand dosing only for men who have sex with men, suited to those averaging fewer than 2 sex acts per week: 2 tablets 2–24 hours before sex, then 1 tablet at 24 and 48 hours after. Women and people with hepatitis B must take it daily. In the on-demand trials, the drug group had more gastrointestinal and kidney adverse effects than placebo, so follow-up can't be skipped. Pilots among MSM began in China in 2019; the 2024 national plan calls for "standardized implementation." No nationwide free policy could be found. Get it prescribed at the infectious-disease or HIV clinic of a designated hospital — call the local CDC first to ask which one. It doesn't protect against syphilis or gonorrhea; keep using condoms, item 30 in this section. After a high-risk event already happened, remedy in Section 13, item 38 (blocking drugs within 72 hours). The beneficiary is mainly you, and it protects your partners too.

Women over 65: get one dual-energy X-ray bone density scan; postmenopausal women with osteoporosis risk factors needn't wait until 65

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Women over 65, and postmenopausal women with osteoporosis risk factors, should get one bone density scan. Screen risk first, then medicate the high-risk: hip fractures fall by about 17%. In absolute terms, about 5 fewer hip fractures per 1,000 people screened. Overall mortality showed no change.

Cost
One DXA scan (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) of lumbar spine and hip at a hospital — minutes lying still. Self-pay usually one to two hundred yuan, varying by region. The heel ultrasound that checkup packages include only screens; it can't diagnose.
Benefit
The US Preventive Services Task Force's 2025 recommendation: screen women 65 and older for osteoporosis (grade B). Also screen postmenopausal women under 65 whose fracture risk is elevated by risk assessment (grade B). For men, evidence was insufficient — no position. The evidence review behind it pooled 3 randomized trials, 42,009 older European women. Screening meant assessing fracture risk first, then DXA for the high-risk, then medication for those found high-risk. Screened groups had about 17% fewer hip fractures. Original value RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.93. In absolute terms, 5 fewer hip fractures per 1,000 screened. One of them, the UK SCOOP trial with 12,483 women aged 70–85, saw hip fractures fall about 28% with screening (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.89), with no mortality difference. The Chinese Medical Association's 2017 guideline suggests bone density measurement for women over 65 and men over 70, and for younger people with one or more osteoporosis risk factors. In the 2017–2018 national survey, osteoporosis prevalence among women over 40 was 20.6%, among men 5.0% (China)
Note
Contested: SCOOP's pre-specified primary outcome was all osteoporotic fractures, and screening didn't significantly reduce those (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.03) — only hip fractures fell. All three trials were "risk assessment first, then DXA"; none isolated DXA alone. The evidence review also estimated that 11.8% to 24.1% of those detected were overdiagnosed — people who would never have fractured from it in their lifetime. Whether men should be screened: the US says evidence insufficient, the Chinese guideline sets it at over 70 — follow your doctor. This entry is about whether your bones can take a fall; falling less is item 13 (balance and leg strength) — do both. What to do after an osteoporosis diagnosis: item 40 (medicate it). The beneficiary is mainly you, and your parents too.

Diagnosed with osteoporosis, or fractured from a trivial fall — get anti-osteoporosis medication prescribed and stay on it; calcium supplements are not a substitute

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

For people already diagnosed with osteoporosis, or who fractured from a minor fall, following the prescribed regimen cuts hip fractures by about half and spinal fractures by more than half. Older patients who start a once-yearly infusion right after hip-fracture surgery have about 35% fewer re-fractures over two years. Calcium alone cannot replace these drugs.

Cost
Prescription needed, taken for years. Common options include a once-weekly tablet and a once-yearly infusion. Bone density is rechecked annually at first, then every 1–2 years once stable. The hard part is staying on it while feeling nothing.
Benefit
A fragility fracture is one caused by minor trauma or ordinary activity. The Chinese Medical Association's 2017 guideline names three groups for medication: those with a prior spine or hip fragility fracture; those with bone density T-score −2.5 or below, fracture or not; and those with low bone mass plus a fragility fracture of wrist, upper arm, or pelvis, or a computed high fracture risk. The guideline also states "current evidence is insufficient to show that calcium alone can replace other anti-osteoporosis drug therapy." Cochrane's 2025 alendronate review: in postmenopausal women with existing osteoporosis or fracture, the drug group had about 51% fewer hip fractures. Original value RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.96. Symptomatic spinal fractures down about 55% (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.73). The HORIZON trial took 2,127 post-hip-fracture-surgery patients, average age 74.5. Starting once-yearly zoledronic acid within 90 days of surgery, median follow-up 1.9 years: new clinical fractures fell from 13.9% to 8.6% — about 35% fewer. Deaths fell from 13.3% to 9.6% — about 28% fewer. The guideline notes that within a year of a hip fracture, about 20% die of complications. In the 2017–2018 national survey, only 1.4% of women with diagnosed osteoporosis or prior fracture were on medication; for men, 0.3% (China)
Note
Contested: a meta-analysis of 38 trials found no reduction in all-cause mortality from these drugs (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.05). Zoledronic acid alone also nonsignificant (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.13). The authors' conclusion: these drugs should be taken to prevent fractures, period. Cochrane's numbers were themselves rated low-to-moderate certainty. For women without a prior fracture and at lower risk, alendronate showed no clear hip-fracture effect (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.32). Rare harms like jaw osteonecrosis and atypical femur fractures aren't fully visible in trials of a few years — hence recheck on schedule and never self-adjust or stop. Some people suit infusions, some tablets; the doctor chooses. For how osteoporosis is found, see item 39 (bone density scan). Menopausal hormone therapy also reduces fractures but is generally considered only when other drugs don't suit. Using hormones for hot flashes: Section 2, item 43. The beneficiary is mainly you, and your parents too.

Drill and measure before stepping onto wild ice; stay off under 15 cm; avoid river ice and ice-fishing holes

Grade CValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

China's official guidance: ice must reach 15 cm thick before adults may skate on it. The US and Canada draw the line at 10 cm — and only for new, clear ice. White ice is half as strong, so double the thickness. On the same sheet, ice a foot thick here can be an inch or two a few steps away — so measure as you go.

Cost
Easiest is a managed, official rink — no extra cost. If you must go on wild ice, bring an ice drill or auger to bore test holes. Also buy a pair of rescue ice picks — two spiked handles worn on the chest. Together, a few dozen to one or two hundred yuan. Measuring every stretch takes time.
Benefit
The China Meteorological Administration's guidance says ice 15 cm thick can carry a skating adult; outdoor rinks also open at 15 cm. Beijing's water authority: official natural rinks need 15 cm of ice, then a week with temperatures between −8°C and 1°C and no strong wind before opening. Wild ice often has holes drilled by fishers that rarely refreeze solidly. Minnesota's DNR guidelines apply to new clear ice only: under 4 inches (about 10 cm), stay off; 4 inches holds a walking person or ice fishing. White ice — snow melted and refrozen — is roughly half as strong: count it at double thickness. On one water body, ice can be a foot thick in one spot and an inch or two a few feet away. Ice over flowing water is usually dangerous — near streams, bridges, and culverts especially; shoreline ice may be thinner than mid-lake. The US National Weather Service also uses 4 inches for walking, ice fishing, and skating. Canada's CCOHS relays the Canadian Red Cross: 15 cm for group skating or walking, 20 cm for large skating parties. These are safety guidelines; no study counts how many deaths compliance prevents (national / US, Canada)
Note
Official guides all say no ice is 100% safe — meeting the thickness threshold is a floor, not a guarantee. Early winter as ice forms and early spring as it thaws are the most dangerous. If you fall in: don't strip — heavy clothing traps air and keeps you afloat. Turn back toward the direction you came from; that ice held you. Get your arms onto the surface, dig the picks in, kick your legs, and haul yourself out. Once out, don't stand — roll flat away from the hole, then get warm fast; severe cold injury means a hospital. If someone else falls through, don't run over to grab them — Section 13, item 25 (don't enter the water yourself for a drowning person): call people, call 110, then extend a pole or throw a rope. The beneficiary is mainly you and the children you take onto the ice.

Guard fitted, goggles plus face shield on, both hands on the angle grinder — and never fit a wood saw blade to cut wood

Grade CValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

An angle grinder spins extremely fast; a shattered disc flies, and a wood-saw blade can kick back violently. In two domestic accidents, both machines had saw blades fitted and no guard: one severed a femoral artery, one a carotid — neither survived. Guard, goggles plus shield, both hands steady — these cost almost nothing.

Cost
Goggles plus a face shield, a few dozen yuan. Check the guard and disc before each start, unplug before changing discs — a minute or two extra. The hard part is not removing the guard or working one-handed when it feels like a hassle.
Benefit
The Canadian CCOHS and Workplace Health and Safety Queensland list these practices. Check guard and disc before starting; never use discs with cracks, chips, or deformation. The disc's rated maximum speed must not be below the machine's rated speed. Disc diameter and bore must match the machine. Disconnect power before changing discs. Secure the workpiece. Wear safety glasses or goggles, plus a face shield over them. Hold both handles with both hands, feet planted. Never use a cutting disc for grinding — it shatters more easily. Don't set the tool down before the disc stops completely. Aim sparks and debris where no one stands, and keep flammables away. Queensland's alert: a cutting disc edge is designed for about 70 meters per second. Fitting a 356 mm disc on a 230 mm machine pushes edge speed to at least 120 m/s — the disc shatters easily. In February 2016 a worker there was struck in the chest by fragments from a 230 mm grinder and died of internal injuries. 2 domestic accident reports: in Harbin 2019, a worker swapped the cutting disc for a toothed saw blade and cut wooden boards with no guard; the blade caught his trousers, severed the femoral artery, and he bled to death. In Shenzhen Futian 2024, a worker cutting a wooden door frame with a wood-saw blade, no guard, no side handle; the machine kicked back and severed the carotid. The national standard cited says "do not fit saw chains, wood-carving blades, or toothed saw blades." Korea's 2011–2018 emergency surveillance counted 8,697 injuries from high-speed rotating cutting tools, 4,603 of them angle-grinder-type tools. Hands were injured in 46.4%, head in 23.0%. Versus comparable tools, grinders roughly doubled the odds of severe injury (OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.88–2.29). A Mianyang, Sichuan hospital admitted 36 inpatients with grinder eye injuries over two years; 10 still had best-corrected vision below 0.05 after surgery. A Turkish hospital's 742 acute hand and forearm injuries in one year included 82 from angle grinders — all but 8 off the job, 44% retirees. A Japanese trauma center's 15 grinder injuries of 2017–2018 included 9 from misuse such as fitting saw blades to cut wood; 2 lost whole fingers, 1 lost part of one (Canada, Australia / China / Korea, Turkey, Japan)
Note
C because these practices come from safety-agency guidance and accident investigations; no study counts injuries prevented. The injury data show only how bad the injuries get, and all come from single hospitals or countries. The "medium" benefit is a judgment call: consequences include death, blindness, and amputated fingers, but they land only on the person holding the grinder. The Harbin machine's own manual said no toothed blades, guard required. The worker had a hand saw beside him — wood belongs to woodworking tools like that. Loose clothing, dangling jewelry, and long hair must be secured; they get wound in. Grinding throws dust and noise — for respirators and earplugs see Section 19, item 10 (employers must supply protective equipment). If a major vessel is cut, press hard on the wound first — Section 13, item 12 (press hard with your hands on major bleeding). The beneficiary is mainly you, and the family standing beside you.

Ask the person whose mood has changed, directly: "Have you thought about suicide?" Asking doesn't plant the idea

Grade BValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: small

The fear that mentioning suicide plants the idea didn't show up in research. Adding suicide questions to student questionnaires left respondents no worse off, and didn't increase suicidal thinking. Depressed kids asked directly actually felt less distressed, and kids with past attempts reported less suicidal ideation.

Cost
Free. One question, then time to listen. The hard part is opening your mouth — many fear that asking will somehow summon the thought.
Benefit
2,342 students across 6 New York high schools were randomized by classroom: one arm's questionnaire included suicide questions, the other's didn't. Right after and 2 days later, distress levels didn't differ (P = .66 and P = .41 — P above 0.05 means no detectable difference). 2 days on, 4.7% of the asked group vs 3.9% of the unasked reported suicidal ideation — no difference (P = .49). Students with pre-existing depression felt less distress when asked (P = .01). Students with past attempts reported less ideation when asked (P = .02). A 2022 meta-analysis reviewed 17 studies and pooled 8 asked-vs-not comparisons: after asking, suicidal ideation and behavior, non-suicidal self-harm, and psychological distress showed no significant increase. The strongest evidence: 8 randomized controlled trials at low or unclear bias risk. A 2014 literature review likewise found no study where asking significantly increased suicidal ideation
Note
Why B: these studies prove only that asking does no harm — none counts how many suicide deaths asking prevents. The "small" benefit likewise reflects the absence of mortality numbers, with only the surrogate endpoint "ideation didn't increase." The asking in these studies was mostly questionnaires and research interviews, not family or friends asking face to face — carrying it to face-to-face is inference. If the answer is yes, don't walk away: stay, call 12356 together, move medications and pesticides out of reach — item 25 in this section (call 12356 when suicidal thoughts appear). If they mention taking others along, or already have means prepared, close relatives can take them directly to a hospital or call 110 — Section 8, item 15. From thought to attempt is often only dozens of minutes — item 32 here (tell one person the moment the thought appears). The beneficiary is mainly spouses and immediate family, but friends and colleagues can ask too.
Sources (3 references)
Gould MS, Marrocco FA, Kleinman M, Thomas JG, Mostkoff K, Cote J, Davies M (2005). Evaluating iatrogenic risk of youth suicide screening programs: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA, 293(13), 1635-1643. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.293.13.1635；Polihronis C, Cloutier P, Kaur J, Skinner R, Cappelli M (2022). What's the harm in asking? A systematic review and meta-analysis on the risks of asking about suicide-related behaviors and self-harm with quality appraisal. Archives of Suicide Research, 26(2), 325-347. https://doi.org/10.1080/13811118.2020.1793857；Dazzi T, Gribble R, Wessely S, Fear NT (2014). Does asking about suicide and related behaviours induce suicidal ideation? What is the evidence? Psychological Medicine, 44(16), 3361-3363. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0033291714001299

2. Don't die slowly

44 entries

This section takes only two kinds of chronic risks: those with a large effect on overall mortality, and those with hard evidence. Entries are ranked by value, highest first. A few are marked "randomized trial," meaning people were randomly split into two groups — the most trustworthy kind of result. The other numbers come from studies that only tracked and recorded, without assigning groups. The HRs and RRs such studies produce carry two confounds: these people differed to begin with, and some changed behavior because they were already ill. So those numbers indicate direction and rough size only — they are not a promise that doing the thing lowers your risk by that much. Entries in this section are grouped by theme, with item numbers in parentheses. Tobacco, alcohol, betel nut: quit smoking, the earlier the better (item 1), no smoking at home or in the car (item 2), get medication first when quitting (item 3), set a quit date (item 4), go to a cessation clinic or call 12320 (item 5), consider e-cigarettes only if you can't quit (item 6), don't chew betel nut (item 8), drink little or none (item 19), if your hands shake when you stop, don't tough it out alone (item 20), count your weekly drinks (item 21). Eat and drink less of: no sugary drinks (item 7), less processed meat (item 18), fewer ultra-processed foods (item 28), no scalding-hot tea or soup (item 30). Swap in and eat more of: switch to low-sodium salt (item 9), a small handful of nuts daily (item 22), swap red meat for fish and poultry (item 23), swap refined grains for whole grains (item 24), tea three or more times a week (item 25), three to four cups of coffee a day (item 26), 5 servings of fruit and vegetables (item 27), chili four or more times a week (item 33), one or two servings of dairy a day (item 34), eggs need not be avoided (item 35). Exercise and weight: walk 7,000–8,000 steps a day (item 11), racket sports (item 14), accumulate bits of vigorous activity (item 15), strength training weekly (item 16), don't sit too long unbroken (item 17), keep BMI at 20–25 (item 32), count the daily dog walk (item 44). Sleep and night shifts: about 7 hours a night (item 13), naps within half an hour (item 37), catch up on sleep the day after a late night (item 38), transfer out of night shifts as early as you can (item 39). Kitchen oil and smoke: don't burn coal or wood for cooking or heating (item 29), don't buy loose machine-pressed peanut oil (item 40), vegetable oil instead of lard and butter (item 41), run the range hood when stir-frying (item 42). Teeth, medication, other habits: brush thoroughly and clean between teeth (item 10), take prescribed medication regularly (item 12), get daylight when out by day (item 31), bathe when you can (item 36), for menopausal hot flashes, get evaluated for hormone therapy (item 43).

1

Quit smoking — the earlier the better

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: yesBenefit: large

Smokers live more than ten years less than non-smokers on average. Quitting before 40 wipes out about 90% of the excess death risk from continuing to smoke. The earlier you quit, the more you get back. And after a bone fracture, keeping smoking makes non-union — the bone failing to knit — about 2.3 times as likely, so don't smoke until the bone has healed.

Cost
Free, and it saves money — a pack a day runs about 20–30 yuan, which stays in your pocket once you quit. The hard part is riding out withdrawal, typically weeks to months.
Benefit
A US cohort study (record-only, no group assignment) found: current smokers lose more than 10 years of life expectancy versus never-smokers. Quitting before 40 eliminates about 90% of the excess mortality from continued smoking. Quitting at 25–34 recovers about 10 years, at 35–44 about 9 years, at 45–54 about 6 years (reported in life-years). Comparable Chinese studies: in the 2010s, urban male smokers died at 1.65 times the rate of non-smokers (RR 1.65), rural males 1.22. Ten years after quitting voluntarily, that smoking-attributable risk nearly vanishes. Same after fractures: pooled across 19 record-only studies, smokers were about 2.3 times as likely to have fracture non-union (OR 2.32, 95% CI 1.76–3.06, adjusted for other factors). Elevated too for tibial and open fractures. In a Swedish randomized trial, of 50 fracture-surgery patients who joined a 6-week cessation program, 20% had at least one postoperative complication; of 55 who didn't, 38%. For surgery scheduled in advance, quitting can start 4–8 weeks pre-op with weekly coaching and nicotine replacement: postoperative complications fall about 58% (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.27–0.65, 2 trials, 210 people).
Note
Other people's smoke kills too: in 2004, about 603,000 deaths worldwide were attributable to second-hand smoke, roughly 1% of global deaths that year. Even if you don't smoke, avoid others' smoke — and above all keep it away from children. How to quit fills the next four entries: item 3 (cessation medication), item 4 (set a quit date), item 5 (cessation clinic), item 6 (e-cigarettes). The non-union figure comes from record-only studies — smokers may differ from non-smokers in other ways that can't all be adjusted away. The post-fracture cessation trial had only 105 people; under another analysis the difference loses significance.
Sources (6 references)
Jha P et al. (2013). 21st-century hazards of smoking and benefits of cessation in the United States. NEJM. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMsa1211128；Chen Z et al. (2015). Contrasting male and female trends in tobacco-attributed mortality in China: evidence from successive nationwide prospective cohort studies. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(15)00340-2；Oberg M et al. (2011). Worldwide burden of disease from exposure to second-hand smoke: a retrospective analysis of data from 192 countries. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)61388-8（二手烟那两个数字）；Scolaro JA et al. (2014). Cigarette smoking increases complications following fracture: a systematic review. J Bone Joint Surg Am. https://doi.org/10.2106/JBJS.M.00081；Nåsell H et al. (2010). Effect of smoking cessation intervention on results of acute fracture surgery: a randomized controlled trial. J Bone Joint Surg Am. https://doi.org/10.2106/JBJS.I.00627；Thomsen T et al. (2014). Interventions for preoperative smoking cessation. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD002294.pub4（骨折和手术那几个数字）
2

Don't smoke at home or in the car — and don't let guests smoke at home

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

About 600,000 people a year die from other people's smoke, nearly three in ten of them children. Long-term second-hand smoke exposure raises hypertension, heart disease, and stroke risk by around 30%. What you breathe at home hurts more than what you breathe outside it.

Cost
Free, no time either. The hard part is speaking up — telling family and guests not to smoke at home.
Benefit
In 2004, 603,000 deaths worldwide were attributable to second-hand smoke, about 1.0% of global mortality, 28% of them children. Pooling 57 studies: those exposed to second-hand smoke had about 1.28 times the odds of hypertension versus the unexposed (odds ratio). Heart disease 1.39, myocardial infarction 1.50, stroke 1.36. Home exposure carries higher risk than exposure outside the home
Note
Start at home: you spend the most time there, and pooled studies show home second-hand smoke is more harmful than exposure elsewhere. Of the health damage from second-hand smoke, 61% lands on children. For quitting yourself, see item 1 in this section.
Sources (2 references)
Öberg M, Jaakkola MS, Woodward A, Peruga A, Prüss-Ustün A (2011). Worldwide burden of disease from exposure to second-hand smoke: a retrospective analysis of data from 192 countries. Lancet: "603,000 deaths were attributable to second-hand smoke in 2004, which was about 1·0% of worldwide mortality. 47% of deaths from second-hand smoke occurred in women, 28% in children, and 26% in men", "61% of DALYs were in children". https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)61388-8；(2026). The Associations Between Secondhand Smoke Exposure and Various Cardiovascular Diseases: A Meta-Analysis. Nicotine & Tobacco Research：57 项研究，"hypertension (OR: 1.28, 95% CI: 1.15 to 1.40), heart disease (OR: 1.39, 95% CI: 1.28 to 1.50), myocardial infarction (OR: 1.50, 95% CI: 1.17 to 1.84), stroke (OR: 1.36, 95% CI: 1.18 to 1.54)" "Home exposure has a higher risk of CVD than non-home exposure". https://doi.org/10.1093/ntr/ntaf111
3

Don't quit on willpower alone — get medication first: it more than doubles your odds

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

Willpower alone fails most people. Those taking varenicline quit at more than twice the rate of placebo. Nicotine replacement — patches, gum — beats no medication by about half. Patch plus gum together adds another 20-odd percent.

Cost
Nicotine patches and gum are over-the-counter at pharmacy counters. A course runs 8–12 weeks, a few hundred to over a thousand yuan. Varenicline and bupropion are prescription-only, from a cessation clinic or respiratory department. The cost roughly cancels against the cigarettes you're not buying.
Benefit
Pooling 41 randomized trials, 17,395 people: the varenicline group's quit rate was 2.32 times placebo's (RR 2.32, 95% CI 2.15–2.51, the confidence interval; high-certainty evidence). Varenicline also beat bupropion (RR 1.36, about 36% higher) and single-form nicotine replacement (RR 1.25, about 25% higher). Nicotine replacement versus nothing: 133 trials, 64,640 people, quit rates about 55% higher (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.49–1.61). A patch plus a fast-acting form (gum, lozenge) beat a single form by about 27% (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.17–1.37, 16 trials, 12,169 people, high-certainty evidence).
Note
The cessation medications sold in China are exactly those three classes; only nicotine replacement is OTC. Varenicline's common effects are nausea, vivid dreams, poor sleep — anyone with psychiatric history must tell their doctor. Nicotine replacement courses run 8–12 weeks; don't stop abruptly on your own, taper as instructed. Medication only covers the misery of withdrawal weeks, not the situations that trigger wanting one — so combine it with item 4 (set a quit date) and item 5 (cessation clinic).
Sources (4 references)
Livingstone-Banks J, Fanshawe TR, Thomas KH, et al. (2023). Nicotine receptor partial agonists for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 5, CD006103. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD006103.pub8；Hartmann-Boyce J, Chepkin SC, Ye W, Bullen C, Lancaster T (2018). Nicotine replacement therapy versus control for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 5, CD000146. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD000146.pub5；Theodoulou A, Chepkin SC, Ye W, et al. (2023). Different doses, durations and modes of delivery of nicotine replacement therapy for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 6, CD013308. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD013308.pub2；上海市卫生健康委员会 (2021). 选对药物，让戒烟轻松一点：「市场上可见的戒烟药物主要有三种，即尼古丁替代疗法药物、安非他酮、伐尼克兰」，「尼古丁替代疗法药物属于非处方药（OTC），可通过药店柜台购买；而安非他酮、伐尼克兰属于处方药，须到医院戒烟门诊或呼吸内科就诊，凭医师处方经药师调配后才能得到」. https://wsjkw.sh.gov.cn/jtyx/20211119/df50681e01ba49f896d54…
4

Set a quit date and stop dead on it — don't taper first

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: yesBenefit: medium

Many plan to cut down a few cigarettes a day and glide to zero. But at six months, 22% of those who set a date and stopped dead hadn't relapsed, versus 15.5% of the taperers. So pick a day, and stop completely on it.

Cost
Free. Just pick a day on the calendar and tell family and colleagues in advance.
Benefit
697 UK smokers were randomized: one arm stopped abruptly on quit day, the other cut consumption by 75% over the preceding two weeks. Both got nurse behavioral support and nicotine replacement before and after quit day. At week 4, 49.0% of the abrupt group (95% CI 43.8–54.2, the confidence range) hadn't relapsed vs 39.2% (34.0–44.4) of the gradual group, relative risk ratio 0.80 (0.66–0.93). At 6 months: 22.0% (18.0–26.6) vs 15.5% (12.0–19.7), relative risk ratio 0.71 (0.46–0.91). Even among those who preferred tapering, week-4 success was lower than among those preferring abrupt stops (38.3% vs 52.2%).
Note
Contested. A dedicated Cochrane review once found the two methods roughly equal (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.79–1.13, 10 trials, 3,760 people), but it was withdrawn in 2019 and no longer updated. So the best current evidence is the randomized trial above, which favors stopping dead. Note also that both arms in that trial started nicotine replacement before quit day — a practice with its own evidence: starting early beats starting on quit day by about 25% (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.08–1.44, 9 trials, 4,395 people, moderate certainty). So the sensible order is: set the date, patch on two weeks early, stop dead on the day.
Sources (2 references)
Lindson-Hawley N, Banting M, West R, Michie S, Shinkins B, Aveyard P (2016). Gradual Versus Abrupt Smoking Cessation: A Randomized, Controlled Noninferiority Trial. Annals of Internal Medicine, 164(9), 585–592. https://doi.org/10.7326/M14-2805；Theodoulou A, Chepkin SC, Ye W, et al. (2023). Different doses, durations and modes of delivery of nicotine replacement therapy for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 6, CD013308（提前用尼古丁替代品那一段）. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD013308.pub2
5

Go to a smoking-cessation clinic, or call 12320 to ask what's available locally

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: mediumWillpower: someBenefit: large

Medication and "someone checking on you regularly" are two different things, and together they work best. People on medication with a dedicated follow-up person quit at nearly twice the rate of those getting only brief advice. Phone counts too: quitlines that call you back proactively raise success by another 20–30%.

Cost
One registration, a few to a few dozen yuan. Behavioral support usually means 4–8 sessions of half an hour to an hour, under 5 hours in total. The hotline is free.
Benefit
Pooling 52 trials, 19,488 people: medication plus behavioral support quit at 1.83 times the rate of usual care or brief advice (RR 1.83, 95% CI 1.68–1.98, the confidence range; high-quality evidence). In the 43 trials recruited at healthcare settings, 1.97 times (1.79–2.18). Telephone counseling alone: among people who had called a quitline themselves, multiple proactive callbacks beat materials-or-one-call by about 38% (RR 1.38, 95% CI 1.19–1.61, 14 trials, 32,484 people); among those who hadn't called, counselor-initiated calls raised success about 25% (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.15–1.35, 65 trials, 41,233 people). Both moderate-certainty evidence.
Note
Finding it in China: search WeChat for the "China Smoking Cessation Platform" mini-program, which lists local quitlines and cessation clinics; or call 12320 to ask whether your area has a clinic. Most of the trials above were done abroad, and clinic intensity varies widely — treat the numbers as direction only. For the medication to pair with it, see item 3 (cessation medication).
Sources (3 references)
Stead LF, Koilpillai P, Fanshawe TR, Lancaster T (2016). Combined pharmacotherapy and behavioural interventions for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 3, CD008286. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD008286.pub3；Matkin W, Ordóñez-Mena JM, Hartmann-Boyce J (2019). Telephone counselling for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 5, CD002850. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD002850.pub4；中国疾病预防控制中心 (2021). 「中国戒烟平台」微信小程序正式上线：「在健康中国行动控烟行动工作组指导下中国疾病预防控制中心和世界卫生组织驻华代表处联合制作了中国权威戒烟资源库『中国戒烟平台』微信小程序。小程序内容主要包括：戒烟热线、戒烟门诊详细信息，以及线上戒烟服务资源等」；同一站点页脚标注「健康咨询电话：12320」. https://www.chinacdc.cn/jkyj/yckz/gzdt/202203/t20220310_296…
6

Consider e-cigarettes only if you've failed to quit; never touch them as a non-smoker

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Switching cigarettes for nicotine e-cigarettes beats nicotine patches by about 60% more successful quits — a solid conclusion. But it isn't harmless, and long-term safety data don't exist yet. For a non-smoker, there is nothing to gain and everything to lose.

Cost
Device plus pods runs a few dozen to a few hundred yuan monthly. Domestically only tobacco flavor is sold, and only at shops holding a tobacco retail license.
Benefit
A continuously updated review included 80 randomized trials, 29,861 people. Nicotine e-cigarettes versus nicotine replacement therapy: quit success about 61% higher (RR 1.61, 95% CI 1.23–2.12, the confidence range; high-certainty evidence, 11 trials, 4,114 people). In absolute terms, roughly 4 extra quitters per 100 (1 to 7 more). Serious adverse events were broadly similar between groups (risk difference 0.01, 95% CI −0.01 to 0.02, moderate certainty). Versus behavioral support alone or none: about 75% higher (RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.39–2.20, low-certainty evidence).
Note
Contested. WHO does not recommend e-cigarettes as a cessation aid, citing insufficient long-term safety data and their role in starting young people on nicotine. The UK puts them in cessation services. China hasn't banned e-cigarettes outright but regulates them tightly under the E-cigarette Administration Measures: only tobacco flavor may be sold — fruit flavors and refillable devices are out; only licensed physical shops may sell; selling via any website, online shop, or social app outside the official national e-cigarette trading platform is illegal; sales to minors prohibited. So fruit-flavored vapes still on sale come through illegal channels outside regulation — that's how "high" vapes spiked with synthetic cannabinoids circulate; see Section 22, item 4 (don't accept pods offered by others). The review tested regulated nicotine products only; mystery-market vape oil isn't covered. Order of attack: try item 3 first (cessation medication) — harder evidence, cheaper too.
Sources (2 references)
Lindson N, Livingstone-Banks J, Butler AR, et al. (2026). Electronic cigarettes for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 8, CD010216. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD010216.pub11；国家烟草专卖局 (2022). 电子烟管理办法（国家烟草专卖局公告 2022 年第 1 号，2022 年 5 月 1 日施行）第十八条：从事电子烟零售业务，要向烟草专卖行政主管部门申领烟草专卖零售许可证。第二十二条：「禁止向未成年人出售电子烟产品。」第二十三条第二款：「任何个人、法人或者其他组织不得通过本办法规定的电子烟交易管理平台以外的信息网络销售电子烟产品、雾化物和电子烟用烟碱等。」第二十六条：「禁止销售除烟草口味外的调味电子烟和可自行添加雾化物的电子烟。」. http://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2022/content_5697988.htm
7

No sugary drinks — and switching to the sugar-free kind isn't a solution either

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

People drinking two or more sweetened bottles a day are about 20% more likely to die over the same period than people who almost never do. One to two a day still adds 10-odd percent. And switching to diet doesn't show a benefit: people drinking two or more artificially sweetened drinks a day run about a quarter higher.

Cost
Free, no time either. Switching to plain water or unsweetened tea saves money. The hard part is breaking the sweet-drink habit, sugar-free versions included.
Benefit
Two large US cohort studies — record-only, no assignment — about 118,000 people and 36,000 deaths. Those drinking 2+ servings daily had about 21% higher mortality than those drinking under 1 a month (HR 1.21). One to two servings daily: about 14% higher (HR 1.14). The European EPIC cohort, also record-only, 450,000 people across 10 countries. Two-plus glasses daily versus under one a month: sugar-sweetened soft drinks about 8% higher (HR 1.08, 95% CI 1.01–1.16). Artificially sweetened (diet) drinks about 26% higher (HR 1.26, 1.16–1.35). All soft drinks pooled: about 17% higher (HR 1.17, 1.11–1.22).
Note
The dispute is over diet drinks. The association for artificially sweetened drinks is stronger than for sugary ones — most likely reverse causation: people already overweight or diabetic are the ones who switch to diet. So don't read this as "sweeteners are more toxic." It does show, though, that "switch to diet and you're fine" has no evidential support. Plain water or unsweetened tea is safest. Also, these studies only track and record — heavy soda drinkers have worse lifestyles overall, so the numbers may be inflated.
Sources (2 references)
Malik VS et al. (2019). Long-Term Consumption of Sugar-Sweetened and Artificially Sweetened Beverages and Risk of Mortality in US Adults. Circulation. https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.118.037401；Mullee A, Romaguera D, Pearson-Stuttard J, et al. (2019). Association Between Soft Drink Consumption and Mortality in 10 European Countries. JAMA Internal Medicine, 179(11), 1479-1490. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2019.2478
8

Don't chew betel nut

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

Betel chewers are about 20% more likely to die over the same period than non-chewers. Diabetes and metabolic syndrome risk run nearly 50% higher. Oral and esophageal cancer risk is on top of that.

Cost
Free, no time, and you save the money spent on betel. The hard part is quitting the chewing habit.
Benefit
Pooling 17 Asian studies, 388,000 people. Betel chewers had about 21% higher mortality than non-chewers (relative risk 1.21, P=0.02). The mortality figure counted 179,600 of them. Diabetes risk about 47% higher (1.47). Metabolic syndrome about 51% higher (1.51). Betel nut is itself a known risk factor for oral and esophageal cancer
Note
The longer you've chewed and the more per day, the higher the oral cancer risk. After quitting, risk drifts down over time. Betel containing tobacco is worse still
Sources (1 references)
Yamada T, Hara K, Kadowaki T (2013). Chewing betel quid and the risk of metabolic disease, cardiovascular disease, and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis. PLoS One, 8(8), e70679. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0070679
9

Swap the household salt for low-sodium (potassium) salt

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

For people who've had a stroke, or over-60s with high blood pressure, switching the household salt to low-sodium salt cuts the 5-year risk of death by about 12% and of stroke by about 14%.

Cost
A bag costs a few yuan more than regular salt. Swap it while shopping — no extra time. Taste barely changes.
Benefit
A randomized trial in rural China, 20,995 people — all either stroke survivors or hypertensives over 60 — followed 4.74 years. The low-sodium-salt group versus regular salt: death risk about 12% lower (RR 0.88). Stroke about 14% lower (RR 0.86). Major cardiovascular events about 13% lower (RR 0.87). Hyperkalemia events showed no statistical difference between groups.
Note
Contested. PURE is a long-running observational study, no assignment. It reported: people excreting under 3 g sodium a day had about 27% higher risk of death plus cardiovascular events; over 7 g a day, about 15% higher. On its numbers, both too little and too much are bad, with the middle best. But in the rural-China randomized trial cited here, low-sodium salt only replaced part of the intake — it doesn't push sodium that low. Note also that the trial subjects were high-risk older people; healthy young people gain much less from switching. Anyone with renal insufficiency, or on potassium-sparing drugs, should ask a doctor before switching.
Sources (2 references)
Neal B et al. (2021). Effect of Salt Substitution on Cardiovascular Events and Death. NEJM. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2105675；O'Donnell M et al. (2014). Urinary sodium and potassium excretion, mortality, and cardiovascular events. NEJM. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1311889（争议方 PURE）
10

Brush thoroughly, clean between your teeth daily, replace missing teeth promptly

Grade BValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

People who clean between their teeth daily with floss or interdental brushes are about 10% less likely to die over the same period. Elders who've lost all their teeth run about 90% higher mortality. Those with fewer than 20 teeth, about double. Electric brushes remove 10–20% more plaque than manual and reduce gum inflammation somewhat — though how much that matters is unclear.

Cost
Floss or interdental brushes run a few dozen yuan a year; a cleaning, one to two hundred each. Two or three extra minutes a day. The hard part is making interdental cleaning a daily habit. If a manual brush doesn't get you clean, an electric one costs a few hundred yuan, with heads to replace periodically.
Benefit
A Japanese study, 9,676 people, 6 years of follow-up. Users of interdental cleaning tools had about 11% lower mortality (hazard ratio 0.89). Users of tongue cleaners, about 23% lower (0.77). Separately, pooled studies of community-dwelling elders: those with no teeth at all had about 1.87 times the odds of death (odds ratio, 95% CI 1.35–2.59, the confidence range). Fewer than 20 teeth: about 2.04 times (1.67–2.49). Electric versus manual: pooling 51 randomized trials, over 1–3 months electric brushing left about 11% less plaque, over 3 months about 21% less. Gingivitis down about 6% and 11% respectively. The review authors say how much these differences matter for health remains unclear
Note
Contested. These studies only track and record. People with bad teeth tend to have worse overall health and finances — whether the teeth drag down the body or the body drags down the teeth can't be disentangled. But the cost is minimal, and periodontitis and missing teeth directly impair eating. Among electric brushes, the round oscillating-rotating heads have the most trials and the clearest edge over manual. Which electric type is best between themselves — the independent reviews declined to say, too few trials. For what an implant costs and which dental procedures insurance covers, see Section 24, item 12 (ask the all-inclusive price before an implant)
Sources (4 references)
Wang K, Matsuyama Y, Kiuchi S, et al. (2026). Routine oral health practices and all-cause mortality. Journal of Dentistry. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdent.2026.106789；Ko MJ, Seo S, So JS, et al. (2026). Deteriorated oral health and function as risk factors for physical disability and mortality in community-dwelling older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. European Geriatric Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41999-025-01319-4；Yaacob M, Worthington HV, Deacon SA, et al. (2014). Powered versus manual toothbrushing for oral health. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD002281.pub3；Deacon SA, Glenny AM, Deery C, et al. (2010). Different powered toothbrushes for plaque control and gingival health. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD004971.pub2
11

Walk 7,000–8,000 steps a day, or accumulate 150–300 minutes of brisk walking a week

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: highWillpower: someBenefit: large

People walking about 7,800 steps a day are roughly 45% less likely to die over the same period than those walking 3,500. By time it's the same story: 150–300 minutes of brisk walking a week beats no exercise by about 30%. Past a certain amount the curve flattens — over 60, 6,000–8,000 steps is enough. Meet either measure and you're covered.

Cost
Free. By step count, that's 60–90 minutes of walking a day, splittable across commutes and errands. By exercise time, 20–45 minutes a day. The hard part is keeping it up for years.
Benefit
Pooling 15 cohort studies — record-only, no assignment — 47,471 people, 3,013 deaths. Quartiles by daily steps; the lowest quartile's median was 3,553 steps/day. The other three medians: 5,801, 7,842, 10,901 steps/day. Their mortality risks ran about 40%, 45%, 53% lower than the lowest (HR 0.60, 0.55, 0.47). For the over-60s, benefits flatten after 6,000–8,000 steps; under 60, after 8,000–10,000. Another pooled analysis: benefit starts from about 3,867 steps/day, and each additional 1,000 steps/day lowers mortality about 15%. By exercise time: pooled cohort studies (record-only) — people at 1–2 times the guideline minimum had about 31% lower mortality than the inactive (HR 0.69). That's 7.5–15 MET·h/week, roughly brisk walking 150–300 min/week. Below the minimum still meant about 20% lower (HR 0.80). At 3–5 times the minimum, about 39% lower (HR 0.61) — the peak. Beyond that, no further drop, but no harm either (10+ times: HR 0.69). Another accelerometer-based pooled study: the most-active quarter had about 48% lower mortality than the least (HR 0.52). An accelerometer is a wearable device that measures movement directly.
Note
Step count and exercise time measure the same thing in different units — meet either one. Going from 4,000 to 7,000 steps is the best-value stretch; no need to force 10,000. Remember these studies only track: among the least active are people already too sick to move — they moved less because they were failing, not the reverse. So the computed gaps run large. The device-measured studies have short follow-up and older participants; the real benefit isn't "risk down to 0.52 times." But the more-you-move-the-better direction is clear.
Sources (4 references)
Paluch AE et al. (2022). Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts. Lancet Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1016/S2468-2667(21)00302-9；Banach M et al. (2023). The association between daily step count and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: a meta-analysis. European Journal of Preventive Cardiology. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurjpc/zwad229；Arem H et al. (2015). Leisure time physical activity and mortality: a detailed pooled analysis of the dose-response relationship. JAMA Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2015.0533；Ekelund U et al. (2019). Dose-response associations between accelerometry measured physical activity and sedentary time and all cause mortality: systematic review and harmonised meta-analysis. BMJ. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.l4570
12

With hypertension or high cholesterol, take your medication as prescribed — don't stop on your own

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

Every 10 mmHg blood pressure comes down, death probability drops about 13% and stroke about 27%. Every 1 unit statins lower LDL cholesterol, death probability drops about 10%. People who take their pills on schedule run 30%–45% lower mortality than frequent missers.

Cost
Volume-procured antihypertensives and statins run a few to a few dozen yuan a month. Once a day, barely any time. The hard part is taking them indefinitely, not stopping when you feel fine.
Benefit
Pooled randomized trials: every 10 mmHg systolic reduction lowers death risk about 13% (RR 0.87). Systolic is the higher blood-pressure number. Major cardiovascular events down about 20% (RR 0.80). Stroke down about 27% (RR 0.73). Heart failure down about 28% (RR 0.72). Statins lower LDL cholesterol: every 1.0 mmol/L drop lowers death risk about 10% (RR 0.90); the same drop lowers major vascular events about 22% (RR 0.78). Separately, pooled cohort studies (record-only): those taking ≥80% as prescribed had lower mortality than frequent missers — statins about 45% lower (RR 0.55), antihypertensives about 29% lower (RR 0.71).
Note
This applies only to people a doctor has judged need medication; healthy people need none. The "adherence" numbers come from tracking — people who adhere are also more self-disciplined overall, which inflates the benefit. The randomized-trial numbers above are more trustworthy. This section has no separate glucose-control entry: the mortality benefit of pushing glucose lower isn't as consistent as for blood pressure and lipids.
Sources (3 references)
Ettehad D et al. (2016). Blood pressure lowering for prevention of cardiovascular disease and death: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(15)01225-8；Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' (CTT) Collaboration (2010). Efficacy and safety of more intensive lowering of LDL cholesterol: a meta-analysis of data from 170 000 participants in 26 randomised trials. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)61350-5；Chowdhury R et al. (2013). Adherence to cardiovascular therapy: a meta-analysis of prevalence and clinical consequences. European Heart Journal. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/eht295
13

Sleep about 7 hours a night, on a fixed schedule

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: highWillpower: someBenefit: medium

People chronically sleeping under 7 hours run about 10% higher mortality over the same period. The more erratic the schedule, the higher the risk. The most regular sleepers run 20% to nearly 50% lower than the least regular. In other words: how regular your sleep is predicts death better than how long it is.

Cost
Free. It takes time — for most people, trading phone-scrolling for sleep. The hard part is fixing your bedtime and wake time.
Benefit
Pooling 16 cohort studies — record-only — 1.38 million people, 113,000 deaths. Short sleepers ran about 12% higher mortality (RR 1.12); long sleepers about 30% higher (RR 1.30). Another pooled analysis by duration band: the 7-hour band had the lowest risk. Below 7 hours, each hour less added about 6% (RR 1.06). Above 7, each hour more added about 13% (RR 1.13). The UK Biobank has wristwatch records for about 61,000 people — record-only. Splitting them into five bands by sleep regularity, the four more-regular bands ran 20%–48% lower mortality than the least regular. Sleep regularity predicts death better than sleep duration. Another UK Biobank study measured sleep timing by wristwatch in 51,562 people, with 3,853 incident cardiovascular diseases. Social jet lag means the gap between weekday and weekend sleep midpoints. Those with 2+ hours of social jet lag ran about 30% higher cardiovascular risk (HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.11–1.54). The association held even among people with normal sleep duration.
Note
What to fix is sleeping too little and sleeping erratically — don't deliberately compress sleep. The high risk among long sleepers is mostly reverse causation: depression, chronic illness, and sleep apnea make people sleep more. Also, the regularity finding currently rests on two cohort studies, record-only — on its own that's Grade B evidence. For recovering after a late night, see item 38 (catch up the very next night).
Sources (4 references)
Cappuccio FP et al. (2010). Sleep duration and all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. Sleep. https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/33.5.585；Yin J et al. (2017). Relationship of Sleep Duration With All-Cause Mortality and Cardiovascular Events: A Systematic Review and Dose-Response Meta-Analysis of Prospective Cohort Studies. JAHA. https://doi.org/10.1161/JAHA.117.005947；Windred DP et al. (2024). Sleep regularity is a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration: A prospective cohort study. Sleep. https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/zsad253；Kumar N, Krishnamurthy S (2026). Social jet lag is associated with incident cardiovascular disease independent of sleep duration and cardiac genetic risk. Journal of Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1111/joim.70133
14

Play racket sports — tennis, badminton, table tennis

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: mediumWillpower: someBenefit: large

Regular racket-sport players run about half the mortality of non-players over the same period, and 56% lower cardiovascular death. Swimmers run about 28% lower. Running and football showed no difference in this dataset.

Cost
Court fees run a few dozen yuan a session. About 2 hours a week. The hard part is rounding up people and a court, every week.
Benefit
A UK cohort of 80,306 comparing participants in a sport with non-participants in it. Racket-sport players (tennis, badminton, table tennis) had about 47% lower mortality (hazard ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.40–0.69, the confidence range). Cardiovascular death about 56% lower (0.44, 0.24–0.83). Swimmers: 0.72 and 0.59 respectively; aerobics 0.73 and 0.64; cycling 0.85. Running and football showed no statistical difference
Note
Contested. These studies only track. People who play sports are healthier to begin with, and more social. That runners showed no difference here also hints that "what kind of person picks what sport" is doing some of the work. Don't conclude running is useless from this entry — this section has entries that count total exercise volume
Sources (1 references)
Oja P, Kelly P, Pedisic Z, et al. (2017). Associations of specific types of sports and exercise with all-cause and cardiovascular-disease mortality: a cohort study of 80 306 British adults. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 51(10), 812-817. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2016-096822
15

Accumulate bits of vigorous effort — stairs, hurrying on foot — to 4–5 minutes a day

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

For people who do no dedicated exercise at all, just having 3 one-to-two-minute bursts of vigorous effort a day — think stair climbs, hurrying somewhere on foot — runs about 40% lower mortality than none, and nearly 50% lower cardiovascular death.

Cost
Free, and no extra workout time to carve out. The hard part is remembering to take the stairs and walk faster rather than saving effort.
Benefit
A UK Biobank study followed 25,200 people who did no dedicated exercise, average 6.9 years, 852 deaths. Some had 3 daily bursts of 1–2 minutes of incidental vigorous activity. Versus none, their all-cause and cancer mortality ran 38%–40% lower, cardiovascular death 48%–49% lower. Those accumulating 4.4 minutes of such activity daily ran 26%–30% lower all-cause and cancer mortality, and 32%–34% lower cardiovascular death
Note
Contested. This study measured activity with wearables — more reliable than questionnaires. But it is still record-only, no trial, and just 6.9 years of follow-up. The subjects were non-exercisers; people already exercising regularly don't need this entry
Sources (1 references)
Stamatakis E, Ahmadi MN, Gill JMR, et al. (2022). Association of wearable device-measured vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity with mortality. Nature Medicine, 28, 2521-2529. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-022-02100-x
16

Do 30–60 minutes of strength training a week

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: mediumWillpower: someBenefit: medium

People training strength 30–60 minutes a week run 10–20% lower mortality than non-trainers over the same period. More doesn't help further. Strength plus aerobic together works best.

Cost
Bodyweight squats and push-ups are free. 1–2 sessions a week, 20–30 minutes each. The hard part is putting it in the weekly schedule.
Benefit
Pooled cohort studies (record-only): strength trainers run 10%–17% lower mortality than non-trainers. More isn't better — the largest reduction, about 10%–20%, sits at roughly 30–60 minutes a week, with no extra benefit beyond. Those doing both strength and aerobic run lower mortality than those doing neither.
Note
These studies only track, and exercise volume was self-reported. The evidence for "overtraining turns harmful" is weak — don't restrict your volume on that account. Strength training also protects older people against falls and muscle loss; that's in Section 1.
Sources (1 references)
Momma H et al. (2022). Muscle-strengthening activities are associated with lower risk and mortality in major non-communicable diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies. British Journal of Sports Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2021-105061
17

Don't sit too long unbroken — get up and move at intervals

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

The longest sitters run 2.6 times the mortality of the shortest over the same period. Long unbroken sitting spells add a separate risk. But 60–75 minutes of moderate activity a day essentially cancels the extra sitting risk.

Cost
Free; standing up a few times costs little time. The hard part is losing track once seated — set a reminder.
Benefit
A US cohort, record-only, measured with accelerometers. Splitting people into quartiles by total daily sitting: the top quartile ran 2.63 times the mortality of the bottom (HR 2.63). Splitting instead by longest unbroken bout: the top quartile ran 1.96 times the bottom (HR 1.96). So total sitting and bout length each associate independently. A separate pooled analysis of over a million people, record-only: those sitting 8+ hours a day with almost no exercise ran 1.59 times the mortality (HR 1.59) of those sitting under 4 hours and most active. About 60–75 minutes of moderate activity daily offsets the excess sitting risk — even the most active sitting 8+ hours showed HR 1.04, no statistical difference.
Note
The solid conclusion: how much you move matters more than how long you sit; with enough exercise, sitting risk largely disappears. Remember these studies only track — the longest sitters include many already ill, so "risk up to 2.63×" clearly contains some "sick first, sat more." Also, in the same pool, 3+ hours of daily TV carried risk at every activity level; the most active just pushed the threshold to 5 hours.
Sources (2 references)
Diaz KM et al. (2017). Patterns of Sedentary Behavior and Mortality in U.S. Middle-Aged and Older Adults: A National Cohort Study. Annals of Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.7326/M17-0212；Ekelund U et al. (2016). Does physical activity attenuate, or even eliminate, the detrimental association of sitting time with mortality? A harmonised meta-analysis of data from more than 1 million men and women. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(16)30370-1
18

Eat less processed meat (ham, bacon, sausage, luncheon meat)

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

The heaviest eaters of ham, bacon, and sausage run about 20% higher mortality than the lightest over the same period. Each extra daily serving of processed meat adds about that much again.

Cost
Free — even saves money — and takes no time. The hard part is cutting back a favorite.
Benefit
Pooled cohort studies (record-only): the highest processed-meat group ran about 23% higher mortality than the lowest (RR 1.23). Total red meat: about 29% higher (RR 1.29). Unprocessed red meat: about 10% higher (RR 1.10), but that one showed no statistical difference. Another pool computed per daily amount: each extra serving of processed meat daily, about 23% higher mortality (RR 1.23); each extra serving of red meat, about 10% (RR 1.10).
Note
Contested. The NutriRECS guideline, using the standard GRADE scoring, rated these studies as less than reliable, and offered only a weak suggestion to keep eating as you do. The dispute is over how hard the evidence is, not the direction. No study finds processed meat beneficial. Unprocessed red meat's effect is smaller and statistically indistinct. The thing to rein in is processed meat.
Sources (3 references)
Larsson SC, Orsini N (2014). Red meat and processed meat consumption and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis. American Journal of Epidemiology. https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwt261；Schwingshackl L et al. (2017). Food groups and risk of all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. https://doi.org/10.3945/ajcn.117.153148；Johnston BC et al. (2019). Unprocessed Red Meat and Processed Meat Consumption: Dietary Guideline Recommendations From the NutriRECS Consortium. Annals of Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.7326/M19-1621（争议方 NutriRECS 指南）
19

Drink little, or not at all

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

Past 100 g of pure alcohol a week, the more you drink, the earlier you die. 100 g of pure alcohol is about 2.5 L of beer. At 40, drinking 100–200 g a week costs roughly half a year of life; 200–350 g, one to two years; over 350 g, four to five years. Counting overall health, the best-value amount is none.

Cost
Free — saves money — and takes no time. The hard part is a moment of awkwardness declining at social occasions.
Benefit
Pooling 83 prospective studies, record-only, 600,000 current drinkers. Mortality's lowest point sits at or below 100 g pure alcohol weekly — roughly 2.5 L of 5% beer, or 300 mL of 40% spirits. At age 40, 100–200 g weekly costs about 6 months of life expectancy; 200–350 g, 1–2 years; over 350 g, 4–5 years (reported in life-years). The Global Burden of Disease study GBD 2016, pooling all health damage, put the lowest-risk drinking level at 0 drinks/week. And one pool corrected for design biases: versus lifetime abstainers, 1.3–24 g daily ran about 7% lower mortality (RR 0.93) — no statistical difference. 45–64 g daily ran about 19% higher (RR 1.19); 65 g and up, about 35% higher (RR 1.35).
Note
Contested. The "a little is good" side is a pool of 34 long cohorts reporting up to 17%–18% lower total mortality among light drinkers, with limits of 4 drinks daily for men and 2 for women, below which heavier drinkers died less. The other side argues the "abstainer" group mixes in ex-drinkers who quit for illness and the constitutionally frail. A pool that specifically removed those confounds found the protection vanished once they were gone. The GBD also puts zero as safest. The safe reading: light drinking won't visibly shorten life; heavy drinking certainly will. "Start drinking for your health" has no basis. For cutting down, see item 21 (count first, then talk to a doctor). Daily drinkers who shake when they stop must not quit cold: item 20.
Sources (4 references)

JAMA Network Open. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.6185；Di Castelnuovo A et al. (2006). Alcohol dosing and total mortality in men and women: an updated meta-analysis of 34 prospective studies. Archives of Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1001/archinte.166.22.2437（争议方）
20

Daily drinkers whose hands shake and heart races when they stop: don't tough it out alone

Grade BValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: mediumWillpower: someBenefit: large

Heavy daily drinkers who stop abruptly get withdrawal. Mild: tremor, sweating, palpitations, insomnia. Severe: seizures or delirium tremens — a medical emergency that kills. Norway followed over 30,000 people; among those who'd had delirium tremens, 8% died each year afterward. If you want to quit, go to a hospital first and say exactly how much you drink daily.

Cost
One psychiatry or addiction-medicine registration, a few to a few dozen yuan. Severe cases need a few days in hospital.
Benefit
A 2026 clinical review states plainly: after abrupt cessation or major reduction, long-term heavy drinkers develop withdrawal syndrome — tremor, autonomic hyperactivity, anxiety, insomnia, perceptual disturbances, seizures, and delirium tremens — "common and potentially life-threatening" in ordinary medical practice. The Norwegian national register cohort covered 36,287 people diagnosed 2009–2015 with alcohol dependence, withdrawal state, or delirium tremens: annual mortality 8.0% in the delirium tremens group, 5.0% in withdrawal state, 3.6% in dependence. The delirium tremens group's standardized mortality ratio was 9.8 (95% CI 8.9–10.7, the confidence range) — about 9.8 times the death rate of age-matched peers.
Note
Self-check: drinking nearly every day; a day off brings tremor, sweat, racing heart, insomnia; needing a morning drink to feel right — any one of these means don't stop alone. The hospital routine is benzodiazepines to carry you through the days, plus thiamine (vitamin B1). Grade B because the Norwegian cohort shows what happens after delirium tremens, not what happens after quitting cold — the connection is inference. The quitting still needs doing; just do it in a hospital. For what counts as heavy: item 19. For cutting down: item 21.
Sources (2 references)
Caputo F, Lungaro L, Costanzini A, De Giorgio R, Addolorato G (2026). Alcohol withdrawal syndrome in hospitalized patients: a practical review. European Journal of Internal Medicine, 107103. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejim.2026.107103；Bramness JG, Heiberg IH, Høye A, Rossow I (2023). Mortality and alcohol-related morbidity in patients with delirium tremens, alcohol withdrawal state or alcohol dependence in Norway: A register-based prospective cohort study. Addiction, 118(12), 2352–2359. https://doi.org/10.1111/add.16297
21

To drink less: first count a week's worth, then talk with a doctor for a few minutes

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: small

A doctor spending a few minutes reviewing your drinking, spelling out the risks, and setting a goal gets you, a year later, 20 g less pure alcohol a week on average — about half a liter of beer. Longer talks add nothing. For those who can't stop, two drugs proven abroad help: roughly 1 in 12 treated no longer returns to heavy drinking.

Cost
Free. Counting drinks is a daily note. Asking at a clinic visit costs nothing extra.
Benefit
Pooling 34 randomized trials, 15,197 people: brief-intervention recipients drank 20 g less pure alcohol per week a year later than minimal-or-no-intervention controls (95% CI 12 to 28 g less, the confidence range; moderate-quality evidence). Baseline intake in these studies averaged 244 g weekly. Brief intervention means advice or lifestyle counseling in no more than 5 sessions totaling under 60 minutes; longer talks added nothing. Drugs: pooling 122 randomized trials, 22,803 people — acamprosate: for every 12 treated (95% CI 8 to 26), 1 extra person returned to no drinking at all; oral naltrexone 50 mg daily: for every 12 treated (8 to 26), 1 extra person avoided returning to heavy drinking.
Note
Benefit is "small" because both lines of evidence measure drinking amounts, not mortality — surrogate endpoints only, by this book's rule. The drug trials were mostly abroad, subjects mostly already meeting dependence criteria, all with psychosocial support bundled in — the numbers are the extra benefit on top. Whether these two drugs are indicated and prescribable in China follows the doctor and the label; don't self-order online. If withdrawal has already appeared, see item 20 (don't quit cold).
Sources (2 references)
Kaner EF, Beyer FR, Muirhead C, et al. (2018). Effectiveness of brief alcohol interventions in primary care populations. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2, CD004148. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD004148.pub4；Jonas DE, Amick HR, Feltner C, et al. (2014). Pharmacotherapy for adults with alcohol use disorders in outpatient settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA, 311(18), 1889–1900. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2014.3628
22

Eat a small handful of nuts a day

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Regular nut eaters run about 20% lower mortality than non-eaters over the same period. Once a week already shows a difference — about 10% lower. A handful a day is where it's most visible.

Cost
28 g a day runs about 200–300 yuan a year. Eaten on the go, no time.
Benefit
Two US cohort studies, 119,000 people, over 3 million person-years. A person-year is people multiplied by years followed each. Versus non-eaters: under once weekly, about 7% lower mortality (hazard ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.90–0.96, the confidence range); once weekly, about 11% (0.89, 0.86–0.93); 2–4 times, about 13% (0.87, 0.83–0.90); 5–6 times, about 15% (0.85, 0.79–0.91); 7+ times, about 20% (0.80, 0.73–0.86)
Note
Buy plain, unsalted. Nuts aren't low-calorie — don't graze on them freely. Remember these studies only follow people; nut eaters have better lifestyles overall, so discount the numbers
Sources (1 references)
Bao Y, Han J, Hu FB, et al. (2013). Association of nut consumption with total and cause-specific mortality. New England Journal of Medicine, 369(21), 2001-2011. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1307352
23

Swap part of your red meat for fish and poultry

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: small

Two extra weekly servings of processed or red meat raise mortality about 3% over the same period. Swap the same servings for fish or poultry and the increase disappears. The effect here is small for this section — do it in passing, don't agonize.

Cost
Free, no time. It's swapping one meat for another, not buying more. The hard part is shifting taste habits.
Benefit
Pooling 6 US cohort studies, nearly 30,000 people. Two extra weekly servings of processed meat: mortality about 3% higher (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 1.02–1.05, the confidence range). Two extra of unprocessed red meat: also about 3% (1.03, 1.01–1.05). The same servings swapped to poultry: 0.99 (0.97–1.02); to fish: 0.99 (0.97–1.01). Neither difference was statistically significant
Note
Two weekly servings move the needle very little — don't expect meat-swapping to buy years. But if you're spending the money anyway, fish and poultry are the better picks
Sources (1 references)
Zhong VW, Van Horn L, Greenland P, et al. (2020). Associations of Processed Meat, Unprocessed Red Meat, Poultry, or Fish Intake With Incident Cardiovascular Disease and All-Cause Mortality. JAMA Internal Medicine, 180(4), 503-512. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2019.6969
24

Swap part of your refined grains for whole grains

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

People eating 90 g more whole grains a day run about 17% lower mortality over the same period. 90 g is about 3 servings. Up to about 200 g a day, it keeps dropping.

Cost
Brown rice, oats, and whole-wheat flour cost a bit more than white; no time. The hard part is adapting to the texture.
Benefit
Pooled cohort studies (record-only): each extra 90 g of whole grains daily lowers mortality about 17% (RR 0.83). 90 g is about 3 servings. The benefit continues to 210–225 g daily. Another pool: each extra daily serving, about 8% lower (RR 0.92).
Note
No need to go all whole-grain — half gets you most of the visible benefit. Remember these studies only track; whole-grain eaters are healthier to begin with, so numbers run large. And the studies disagree widely (I² 83% — the higher, the less consistent).
Sources (2 references)
Aune D et al. (2016). Whole grain consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and all cause and cause specific mortality: systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies. BMJ. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.i2716；Schwingshackl L et al. (2017). Food groups and risk of all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. https://doi.org/10.3945/ajcn.117.153148
25

Drink tea three or more times a week

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Habitual tea drinkers run about 15% lower mortality over the same period. From age 50, that's 1.26 extra years of life on average, and 1.41 extra years free of cardiovascular disease.

Cost
A few dozen to a few hundred yuan a year. Brewing a cup takes minutes.
Benefit
A Chinese study of 100,900 people (China-PAR), half followed a full 7.3 years. Habitual tea drinkers ran about 15% lower mortality (hazard ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.79–0.90, the confidence range). From age 50: tea drinkers got 1.41 more years free of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and 1.26 more years of life expectancy
Note
Contested: these studies only track, and Chinese male tea drinkers smoke and drink more; the authors adjusted for some of it, but not cleanly away. Also, don't drink it scalding — for hot-drink temperature, see this section's entry on it. On mycotoxin worries: of 158 domestic dark-tea samples checked, 2 had detectable aflatoxin, with intake below international acceptable levels at actual drinking amounts. Another survey of 352 samples across 16 mycotoxins found only ochratoxin A in dark tea above limits on average. At Chinese consumption levels, neither computed a dietary risk. Store tea dry; discard damp or moldy leaves. Green tea extract capsules are a different matter: concentrated catechins swallowed in bulk can injure the liver — brewed tea doesn't do this. So this entry means brewed tea only; don't substitute extract supplements
Sources (4 references)
Wang X, Liu F, Li J, et al. (2020). Tea consumption and the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality: The China-PAR project. European Journal of Preventive Cardiology, 27(18), 1956-1963. https://doi.org/10.1177/2047487319894685；茶叶霉菌毒素：Cui P et al. (2020). Quantitative analysis and dietary risk assessment of aflatoxins in Chinese post-fermented dark tea. Food and Chemical Toxicology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fct.2020.111830；Zhou H et al. (2022). Mycotoxins in Tea (Camellia sinensis (L.) Kuntze): Contamination and Dietary Exposure Profiling in the Chinese Population. Toxins. https://doi.org/10.3390/toxins14070452；绿茶提取物与肝损伤：Hu J et al. (2018). The safety of green tea and green tea extract consumption in adults - Results of a systematic review. Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.yrtph.2018.03.019
26

Drink three to four cups of coffee a day, no sugar, no cream

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Three to four cups a day runs about 17% lower mortality than none over the same period.

Cost
Brewing your own runs 1–2 yuan a day. A cup takes minutes.
Benefit
An umbrella review pooled 201 meta-analyses, whose underlying studies were all record-only. Result: 3–4 cups daily versus none, mortality 17% lower (relative risk 0.83, 95% CI 0.79–0.88, the confidence range)
Note
Contested: the authors state the evidence is almost entirely observational, and that "robust randomised controlled trials" would be needed to judge causation — tracking alone can't establish it. Drink it black; sugar and cream toppings cancel the benefit. Pregnant women, and people with arrhythmia, anxiety, or insomnia, skip this entry
Sources (1 references)
Poole R, Kennedy OJ, Roderick P, et al. (2017). Coffee consumption and health: umbrella review of meta-analyses of multiple health outcomes. BMJ, 359, j5024. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.j5024

Eat 5 servings (about 400 g) of fruit and vegetables a day

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: mediumWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Each extra 200 g of fruit and vegetables daily lowers mortality about 10% over the same period. Five servings a day runs about 13% lower than two. Beyond that, no further drop.

Cost
A few to a dozen-odd yuan a day. Washing and cutting take some time daily. The hard part is buying and eating enough every single day.
Benefit
Pooled cohort studies (record-only): each extra 200 g daily, mortality about 10% lower (RR 0.90). The benefit continues to 800 g a day. Two large US cohorts plus a 26-study pool: 5 servings a day ran about 13% lower mortality than 2 (HR 0.87). The best mix was 2 servings of fruit plus 3 of vegetables; more added nothing.
Note
5 servings is enough — no need to push 10; both studies agree on that. Remember these studies only track, with heavy confounding: vegetable eaters differ in income, education, and exercise. So "about 10% lower" is already the ceiling.
Sources (2 references)
Aune D et al. (2017). Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies. International Journal of Epidemiology. https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw319；Wang DD et al. (2021).
