28

Eat fewer ultra-processed foods (chips, instant noodles, pastries, ready meals)

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: highWillpower: yesBenefit: large

The heaviest ultra-processed-food eaters run about 20% higher mortality than the lightest over the same period, and 50% higher cardiovascular death. But this evidence is rated uncertain — discount the numbers accordingly.

Cost
Free — just buy differently. It means cooking yourself, or taking time to pick minimally processed ingredients, every day. The hard part is fighting the inertia of "convenient is fine" long-term.
Benefit
An umbrella review pooled multiple meta-analyses, underlying studies all record-only. High versus low ultra-processed intake: mortality about 21% higher (RR 1.21), cardiovascular death about 50% higher (RR 1.50). These two carried evidence grades of "highly suggestive" and "convincing." But under the standard GRADE scoring, certainty was low or very low.
Note
Contested on three counts. First, the NOVA classification lumps nutritionally very different foods together. Second, it overlaps heavily with sugary drinks and processed meat (items 7, 18) — you can't tell which is doing the work. Third, GRADE rates it low. So after doing those two, how much this one adds is unclear. The counter-evidence is the same review's low rating itself; no primary study reaches the opposite conclusion. Do items 7 and 18 first, then this one.
Sources (1 references)
Lane MM et al. (2024). Ultra-processed food exposure and adverse health outcomes: umbrella review of epidemiological meta-analyses. BMJ. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2023-077310
29

Cook and heat with electricity or gas, not coal or wood

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: highTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: large

People burning coal or wood for cooking run about 10% higher mortality over the same period; for heating, about 14%. Those who've switched to electricity or gas run 13%–33% lower than those still burning solid fuel.

Cost
Rural households need new stoves plus fuel — a few hundred to over a thousand yuan a year. A one-time change. Urban dwellers are mostly there already.
Benefit
A Chinese chronic-disease cohort, record-only, 271,000 adults without cardiovascular disease. Solid-fuel cooks ran about 11% higher mortality than electricity-or-gas users (HR 1.11); solid-fuel heating, about 14% higher (HR 1.14). Those who had switched from solid to clean fuel, versus still burning: cooking about 13% lower (HR 0.87), heating about 33% lower (HR 0.67). Outdoor PM2.5 is a separate account: pooling 104 cohort studies, each 10 µg/m³ of long-term exposure raises natural-cause mortality about 8% (RR 1.08). Natural cause means non-accidental death from illness.
Note
These studies only track. Families that switched fuel are also wealthier, so "risk down to 0.67×" contains some household-income effect. As for outdoor PM2.5, personal options are limited — moving, masks, purifiers. Air purifiers have no mortality-endpoint studies, so this section quotes no numbers.
Sources (2 references)
Yu K et al. (2018). Association of Solid Fuel Use With Risk of Cardiovascular and All-Cause Mortality in Rural China. JAMA. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2018.2151；Chen J, Hoek G (2020). Long-term exposure to PM and all-cause and cause-specific mortality: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Environment International. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2020.105974
30

Let hot things cool a bit — no scalding tea, soup, or coffee

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

Drinking very hot tea carries 8 times the esophageal cancer risk of warm tea. Even "hot" doubles it. Drinking within two minutes of pouring runs 5 times the risk of waiting four minutes or more.

Cost
Free; two or three extra minutes each time. The hard part is holding back when it smells good.
Benefit
In a high-incidence region of northern Iran, 300 patients were compared with 571 without the disease. All versus warm-tea drinkers: "hot" tea carried about 2.07 times the odds of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (odds ratio, 95% CI 1.28–3.35, the confidence range); "very hot," about 8.16 times (3.93–16.9). Drinking within 2 minutes of pouring ran about 5.41 times the odds of waiting 4+ minutes (2.63–11.1)
Note
The IARC classifies beverages above 65 °C as Group 2A — probably carcinogenic. The same assessment cleared coffee itself. China's Chaoshan and Taihang regions have high esophageal cancer rates, tied to the drink-it-scalding habit
Sources (2 references)
Islami F, Pourshams A, Nasrollahzadeh D, et al. (2009). Tea drinking habits and oesophageal cancer in a high risk area in northern Iran: population based case-control study. BMJ, 338, b929. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.b929；Loomis D, Guyton KZ, Grosse Y, et al. (2016). Carcinogenicity of drinking coffee, mate, and very hot beverages. Lancet Oncology, 17(7), 877-878. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1470-2045(16)30239-X

Get daylight when you're out by day — don't live unlit

Grade BValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Women who deliberately avoid the sun lose 0.6–2.1 years of life expectancy versus the most sun-exposed. Non-smokers who avoid the sun live about as long as the heaviest smokers who bask.

Cost
Free. A dozen-odd minutes a day; commutes and lunch breaks cover it.
Benefit
A Swedish study, 29,500 women, 20 years of follow-up. Versus the most-exposed group, deliberate sun-avoiders lost 0.6–2.1 years of life expectancy. The authors wrote that "the avoidance of sun exposure was a risk factor for death of a similar magnitude as smoking"
Note
Contested: Sweden sits at high latitude with weak sun, so the finding doesn't transfer cleanly to China. Sun-avoiders may also be frailer and more housebound to begin with. Don't burn either — cover up at midday, since sun exposure raises skin cancer risk
Sources (1 references)
Lindqvist PG, Epstein E, Nielsen K, et al. (2016). Avoidance of sun exposure as a risk factor for major causes of death: a competing risk analysis of the Melanoma in Southern Sweden cohort. Journal of Internal Medicine, 280(4), 375-387. https://doi.org/10.1111/joim.12496
32

Keep BMI at 20–25; if overweight, lose it

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: highWillpower: yesBenefit: large

Mortality is lowest in the BMI 20–25 band. At 27.5–30 it's about 20% higher; 30–35, about 45%; 35–40, nearly double. East Asians are more sensitive to excess weight: every 5 points of BMI adds about 40% risk.

Cost
Free. Diet and exercise take time daily. This is the section's most willpower-hungry entry: managing intake and moving for the long haul — and keeping it off is harder than losing it.
Benefit
Individual data pooled from 239 prospective studies (record-only). The analysis kept only three kinds of people: never-smokers, those free of chronic disease at enrollment, and those who survived 5+ years after enrollment. Result: mortality lowest at BMI 20–25. BMI 25–27.5: about 7% higher (HR 1.07). 27.5–30: about 20% (1.20). 30–35: about 45% (1.45). 35–40: about 94% (1.94). 40–60: 2.76 times (2.76). Above BMI 25, each extra 5 kg/m² added about 39% for East Asians (HR 1.39).
Note
Contested. One camp holds that "a bit overweight actually prolongs life." Their pool found overweight about 6% lower mortality, mild obesity about 5% lower. The disagreement is mostly over whether to drop three kinds of data: smokers, the already-ill, and the first years after enrollment. They're dropped because the gravely ill lose weight first. Once the 239-study analysis dropped all three, the overweight risk reappeared. Also note: no randomized trial proves that losing weight itself lowers all-cause mortality. The benefit above is a cross-sectional comparison of differently-sized people — not a promise that slimming cuts your risk by that much. If you're losing weight, don't bother with meal timing: breakfast and 16:8 fasting add nothing — see Section 6, item 26 (don't count on breakfast or 16:8 for weight control)
Sources (2 references)
Global BMI Mortality Collaboration (2016). Body-mass index and all-cause mortality: individual-participant-data meta-analysis of 239 prospective studies in four continents. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(16)30175-1；Flegal KM et al. (2013). Association of all-cause mortality with overweight and obesity using standard body mass index categories: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.113905（争议方）

Eat chili four or more times a week

Grade BValue: very highMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: large

People eating chili 4+ times a week run about 23% lower mortality than rare eaters over the same period, and about a third lower cardiovascular death.

Cost
Free, no time.
Benefit
An Italian study of 22,800 people, half followed a full 8.2 years, 1,236 deaths. Chili 4+ times weekly versus rarely: mortality about 23% lower (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.66–0.90, the confidence range). Cardiovascular death about 34% lower (0.66, 0.50–0.86)
Note
Contested: this is record-keeping against a Mediterranean-diet backdrop, and chili eaters may simply eat closer to the local tradition. Also, people with reflux, hemorrhoids, or irritable bowel get worse symptoms from chili — don't force it
Sources (1 references)
Bonaccio M, Di Castelnuovo A, Costanzo S, et al. (2019). Chili Pepper Consumption and Mortality in Italian Adults. Journal of the American College of Cardiology, 74(25), 3139-3149. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2019.09.068

Drink one or two servings of milk or yogurt a day

Grade BValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: large

People having two or more daily servings of milk or yogurt run about 17% lower mortality than non-consumers over the same period.

Cost
A few yuan a day, no time.
Benefit
The PURE cohort spans 21 countries, 136,000 people, average 9.1 years, 6,796 deaths. Two-plus daily dairy servings versus none: mortality about 17% lower (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.72–0.96, the confidence range), trend P=0.0052
Note
Contested: PURE includes many low- and middle-income countries where being able to afford daily dairy itself signals means, and that confound resists cleaning. The lactose-intolerant can switch to yogurt or low-lactose milk — no need to force cow's milk
Sources (1 references)

Eggs needn't be banned — just not three or four a day

Grade BValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: small

Each extra half egg a day adds about 7% mortality over the same period. Swap that half egg for egg whites, fish, poultry, or nuts, and every cause-of-death risk comes out lower. No need to quit eggs — just don't eat three or four daily.

Cost
Free, no time.
Benefit
A US cohort of 521,000 people, 129,000 deaths. Each extra half whole egg daily: mortality about 7% higher (hazard ratio 1.07, 95% CI 1.06–1.08, the confidence range). Swapping that half egg for equal amounts of egg whites, poultry, fish, dairy, or nuts and legumes meant lower mortality — cardiovascular, cancer, and respiratory deaths all lower too
Note
Heavily contested: other large cohorts and pools found no egg–mortality link. The US dietary guidelines dropped the daily cholesterol cap. What to avoid is three or four a day; one a day is nothing to worry about
Sources (1 references)
Zhuang P, Wu F, Mao L, et al. (2021). Egg and cholesterol consumption and mortality from cardiovascular and different causes in the United States: A population-based cohort study. PLoS Medicine, 18(2), e1003508. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1003508
36

Bathe when you can, don't just shower

Grade BValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: mediumWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Near-daily bathers run about 28% lower cardiovascular events than those bathing under twice a week, and about 46% lower brain hemorrhage.

Cost
More water and electricity. Half an hour a soak.
Benefit
A Japanese study of 30,000 people, 19 years, 2,097 cardiovascular events. Near-daily bathing versus at most twice weekly: cardiovascular events about 28% lower (hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.62–0.84, the confidence range). Coronary heart disease about 35% lower (0.65, 0.45–0.94). Stroke about 26% (0.74, 0.62–0.87). Brain hemorrhage about 46% (0.54, 0.40–0.73)
Note
Contested: this comes from a Japanese population and bathtub culture; most Chinese households can't soak daily. Don't overheat the water or soak too long — for the elderly and those with cardiovascular disease, very hot water and long soaks are dangerous, and Japan records many elderly bathtub deaths yearly
Sources (1 references)
Ukai T, Iso H, Yamagishi K, et al. (2020). Habitual tub bathing and risks of incident coronary heart disease and stroke. Heart, 106(10), 732-737. https://doi.org/10.1136/heartjnl-2019-315752
37

Keep naps under half an hour, never past an hour; if you truly need 1–2 hours to function, get checked

Grade BValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Napping under an hour raises neither mortality nor chronic-disease risk, and the mind is sharper. Past an hour: coronary risk up about 30%, diabetes and obesity up about 20%. So set an alarm for half an hour. And if you truly need 1–2 hours daily to function, that's a signal to get examined.

Cost
Free. Set an alarm before dozing off; almost no willpower needed.
Benefit
An umbrella review pooled 16 meta-analyses, 244 health outcomes. An umbrella review re-pools existing pools. Conclusion: naps under 60 minutes raised neither total mortality nor chronic-disease risk, with the clearest cognitive improvement (SMD 0.69, 95% CI 0.37–1.00, the confidence range). Short naps of 20–30 minutes best improved physical performance (SMD 0.99, 0.67–1.31). Naps over 60 minutes: coronary risk about 30% higher, diabetes and obesity about 20% higher. Another study had 1,338 people over 56 wear wristwatches to measure naps directly rather than self-report. Follow-up up to 19 years, 926 deaths. Each extra hour of napping: mortality about 13% higher (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.04–1.23). Each extra daily nap: about 7% higher (HR 1.07, 1.02–1.13). Morning nappers ran about 30% higher than early-afternoon nappers (HR 1.30, 1.03–1.64).
Note
Contested. Both studies are record-only. Long nappers are likelier to have sleep apnea, anemia, hypothyroidism, depression, or other chronic illness. So how much of "long nappers die more" the napping itself causes is unanswerable. Genetic causal inference (Mendelian randomization, 453,000 plus 541,000 people) supports exactly one thing: more frequent napping goes with slightly higher blood pressure and waistline. It found no causal effect of napping on coronary disease or diabetes. So don't treat "nap less" as a mortality reducer. The "get checked" half is author advice, Grade C: if daytime sleepiness forces long naps, check night sleep first — snoring and breathing stops mean a sleep-apnea workup — then blood counts and thyroid. For how a short nap refreshes: Section 3, item 11 (10 minutes when the afternoon slump hits). For night duration: item 13 here.
Sources (3 references)
Du P, Li J, Hua Z, et al. (2026). Multiple Health Outcomes of Daytime Napping: A Comprehensive Umbrella Review. Public Health Reviews. https://doi.org/10.3389/phrs.2026.1609013；Gao C, Cai R, Zheng X, et al. (2026). Objectively Measured Daytime Napping Patterns and All-Cause Mortality in Older Adults. JAMA Network Open. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.7938；Dashti HS et al. (2021). Genetic determinants of daytime napping and effects on cardiometabolic health. Nature Communications. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-20585-3
38

After a late night, catch up the very next night — don't bank it for the weekend

Grade BValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

People who short their sleep and don't make it up the next night run about 15% higher mortality than the regular-scheduled; severely short without catch-up, about 42% higher. Those who caught up showed no elevated risk. So after a late night, go to bed early the next night.

Cost
Free. The catch-up hour or two is sleep you wanted anyway.
Benefit
UK Biobank, 85,618 people, average age 61.8, wristwatch-recorded daily sleep, median 8 years. The study computed "short-sleep nights" per person — 2.5+ hours below one's own need. The first night after a short night counted as the "rebound night," qualifying as caught-up if it exceeded one's need. Five patterns emerged. Versus regular sleepers: short-without-catch-up ran about 15% higher all-cause mortality (HR 1.15, 95% CI 1.01–1.31, the confidence range); cumulative shortfall over 3.5 hours without catch-up, about 42% higher (HR 1.42, 1.24–1.63). Both caught-up groups showed no significant association — short-then-caught-up was HR 1.12 (0.98–1.28). Among habitually short sleepers, short-without-catch-up ran about 19% higher (1.19, 1.01–1.40), severe-without-catch-up about 38% (1.38, 1.17–1.63). The result replicated in a US survey cohort of 4,586.
Note
This is record-only. Those who can't catch up may be busier and sicker to begin with — not fully cleanable. "Caught-up groups showed no elevated risk" means no difference was detected; their point estimates still exceed 1, so catching up isn't a license. Repay late nights promptly, and don't treat that as permission to burn them freely. Catch-up here means the first night after a short one — not banking it for the weekend. Making "short weekdays, weekend catch-up" a weekly rhythm is social jet lag, itself tied to cardiovascular disease — see item 13 (about 7 hours, fixed schedule). The fixed-weekend-waketime entry is Section 3, item 2 — no conflict: this one says go to bed early the next night, not sleep till noon.
Sources (1 references)
Li X, Zhang M, Li Z, et al. (2026). Acute sleep rebound following sleep restriction is associated with reduced mortality risk. Nature Communications. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72461-1
39

The longer you work night shifts, the higher the cardiovascular risk — transfer out as early as you can

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: highTime: mediumWillpower: yesBenefit: large

Night-shift workers have about 13% more cardiovascular disease than non-shift, and about 27% more cardiovascular death. It scales with years: every 5 more years of nights adds roughly 7% more disease. So this account is settled in years — transfer early if you can. As for shift work causing cancer, the evidence is far softer than the lore.

Cost
Transferring or changing jobs may cut pay and lose the shift allowance. Job-hunting takes time and resolve. If you're choosing a job and price this in up front, the cost is zero.
Benefit
Pooling 23 cohort studies, record-only. Night-shift workers: cardiovascular events about 13% higher (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.10–1.16, the confidence range). Cardiovascular death about 27% higher (RR 1.27, 1.18–1.36). By years: every 5 more years of night shifts added about 7% more cardiovascular disease (RR 1.07, 1.04–1.09) and about 5% more cardiovascular death (RR 1.05, 1.03–1.06). By disease: coronary incidence about 22% higher (1.22, 1.16–1.28), coronary death about 22% (1.22, 1.10–1.36), ischemic heart disease death about 39% (1.39, 1.06–1.84), stroke death about 49% (1.49, 1.04–2.12). Stroke incidence was nonsignificant (1.06, 0.95–1.18).
Note
All record-only. Night workers differ in smoking, weight, and income, never fully adjusted away. On night shifts causing cancer, the evidence is much softer than the lore: in a pool of 12 studies, 12,132 breast cancers, ever-shift workers ran just 5% higher with a confidence range crossing 1 (RR 1.05, 0.96–1.14). The 20-year-plus band ran 25% higher (1.25, 1.01–1.55), but that lost significance under influence analysis and neared 1 after publication-bias adjustment — the authors called the association "far from established." A Chinese cohort of men followed 16.1 years, 8,202 cancers, found no link between night shifts and total or most common cancers; only pancreatic cancer in the 11–20 cumulative-year band ran about 59% higher (HR 1.59, 1.09–2.31). So this entry settles accounts on cardiovascular grounds, not cancer. Not everyone should quit nights — the year-count account is yours to run. If you're staying, fix what's fixable: smoking, item 1; blood pressure and lipids, item 12; sleep recovery after shifts, item 38. Two tactics to try: concentrate eating into daytime, and shift the body clock with bright light plus strict daytime darkness — the only method proven to actually move the clock. Under ordinary indoor lighting, six consecutive night shifts leave the clock unmoved; with 7,000–12,000 lux bright light plus near-total daytime darkness, it inverts fully in four days. Bright enough light at night, strict blackout for day sleep, and sunglasses against morning light on the way home — all three, or it doesn't work; skip the last one and it's wasted. Both tactics' endpoints reach only metabolic markers and sleep; no trial measured whether they cut cardiovascular risk. Living days again on rest days pushes the clock back. Doses, original numbers, further sources, and how the body tells time are in [docs/生物钟和夜班.md](../docs/生物钟和夜班.md).
Sources (4 references)
Xi J, Ma W, Tao Y, et al. (2025). Association between night shift work and cardiovascular disease: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1668848；Esposito G, Bravi F, Santucci C, et al. (2025). Night shift work and breast cancer risk in healthcare workers: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Occupational Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1093/occmed/kqaf040；Shen QM, Li ZY, Tan YT, et al. (2026). Night shift work and risk of total and site-specific cancer: results from a prospective cohort study among Chinese men. Scandinavian Journal of Work, Environment & Health. https://doi.org/10.5271/sjweh.4290；Czeisler CA, Johnson MP, Duffy JF, et al. (1990). Exposure to bright light and darkness to treat physiologic maladaptation to night work. New England Journal of Medicine, 322(18), 1253-1259. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199005033221801
40

Buy prepackaged cooking oil with an SC number — not loose workshop-pressed peanut oil

Grade BValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Damp, moldy peanuts grow aflatoxin, a definite carcinogen that hits the liver hardest. After Guangzhou tightened workshop rules, residents who often ate home-pressed oil had about 35% fewer abnormal liver-function readings. Guangxi mothers-to-be eating home-pressed peanut oil ran about 90% higher risk of low birth weight and about 80% higher preterm birth.

Cost
Same money, different shelf. Check the pack for an SC-prefixed food-production license number. The hard part is persuading elders who always buy home-pressed oil.
Benefit
Aflatoxin is an IARC Group 1 carcinogen (definitely causes human cancer), mainly liver. A Guangzhou study measured aflatoxin B1 in workshop-pressed peanut oil, 2010–2022. Median 1.29 μg/kg, middle half of samples between 0.12 and 6.58. After local workshop regulations took effect, toxin levels immediately dropped 2.865 μg/kg, then another 2.593 yearly. Abnormal liver function among residents of the high-consumption area fell accordingly (PR 0.650, 95% CI 0.469–0.902, the confidence range) — about 35% lower. A Guangxi cohort of 1,611 pregnant women: 81.7% ate home-pressed peanut oil. Their babies ran about 90% higher risk of low birth weight (aOR 1.9, 1.1–3.2) and about 80% higher preterm birth (aOR 1.8, 1.1–3.0).
Note
Both studies are record-only without controls. Guangzhou's endpoint was liver-function labs, not liver cancer or death. Home-pressed oil's median toxin actually sits below the national 20 μg/kg limit for peanut oil — the risk is in decades of eating it plus the occasional hot batch. The national limit applies to all peanut oil, but prepackaged oil passes production licensing and factory testing; workshops are governed by provincial rules with far less sampling. The beneficiary is mainly you and everyone at your table.
Sources (3 references)

Cook with vegetable oil instead of lard and butter; don't shop oils for health, and don't expect flaxseed oil to protect your heart

Grade AValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Eating less saturated fat — lard, butter — and swapping in vegetable oil cuts heart attacks and strokes by about 17%, but total mortality doesn't budge. Soybean, corn, and canola oils are interchangeable — no evidence separates them. Flaxseed oil in quantity shows no drop in heart disease either.

Cost
No extra money. Vegetable oil is most households' default anyway. The hard part is giving up the lard stir-fry taste.
Benefit
Cochrane pooled 15 randomized trials, 56,675 people, each running at least 2 years. Less saturated fat: combined cardiovascular events about 17% lower (RR 0.83, 0.70–0.98). Total mortality essentially unchanged (RR 0.96, 0.90–1.03), cardiovascular death too (RR 0.95, 0.80–1.12). Replacing with polyunsaturated fat (the bulk of soybean and corn oil) versus carbohydrates: no detectable difference. Monounsaturated (canola, olive): too little data. Another Cochrane pool, 19 trials, 6,461 people: extra omega-6 (linoleic acid) — total mortality RR 1.00 (0.88–1.12), cardiovascular events RR 0.97 (0.81–1.15): no benefit, no harm. A third pool, 86 trials, 162,796 people: extra plant omega-3 (flaxseed and perilla oil) — total mortality RR 1.01 (0.84–1.20), coronary events RR 1.00 (0.82–1.22): essentially nothing.
Note
Contested: some argue the omega-6 in soybean and corn oil is pro-inflammatory, so eat less or switch. The omega-6 randomized trials above show no harm, at self-rated low quality. The benefit is sized "medium" on the 17% event reduction; total mortality didn't move. Whatever the oil, control the amount — the dietary guideline says 25–30 g of cooking oil per person per day.
Sources (3 references)
Hooper L, Martin N, Jimoh OF, et al. (2020). Reduction in saturated fat for cardiovascular disease. Omega-6 fats for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (11), CD011094. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD011094.pub4；Abdelhamid AS, Brown TJ, Brainard JS, et al. (2020). Omega-3 fatty acids for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease. 42

Run the range hood from the moment you fire up until you finish cooking or frying

Grade BValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

Non-smoking Chinese women who rarely or never run the hood while stir-frying run about double the lung cancer risk of habitual users. Living in a home with a poorly ventilated kitchen adds about 50%, most visibly in coal-burning households.

Cost
If you have a hood, a little electricity. If not, buying and installing one runs a few hundred to over a thousand yuan. The hard part is turning it on every single time and not switching it off because it's loud.
Benefit
Pooling 10 case-control studies of non-smoking Chinese women. Case-control compares patients with the healthy and asks about past habits. Cooking-oil-fume exposure carried about 1.74 times the odds of lung cancer (odds ratio, 95% CI 1.57–1.94, the confidence range). The 4 studies isolating fume exposure without a hood: about 2.11 times (1.54–2.89). A Taiwanese study matched 1,302 non-smoking female lung cancer patients with 1,302 healthy women, restricted to 10+ years of cooking. Hood use in over two-thirds of those years versus under a third: risk about halved (odds ratio 0.49, 0.32–0.76). A Shanghai cohort followed 71,000 non-smoking women from 1996 to 2009, finding 429 lung cancers. Self-reported living in poorly ventilated kitchens: about 49% higher risk (HR 1.49, 1.15–1.95). Coal plus poor ventilation for 20+ years: about 2.03 times (HR 2.03, 1.35–3.05). Coal alone showed no difference (HR 1.03, 0.84–1.26). Cooking-oil type: no difference either.
Note
Contested: the pro-hood numbers come mostly from case-control studies. Patients recalling the past after diagnosis tend to under-report hood use, inflating the numbers. In the Shanghai cohort, the elevated risk concentrated in coal-plus-poor-ventilation homes; gas-only homes got no separate number. Hence only Grade B, with the benefit sized "large" on the roughly-twofold risk difference. For not burning coal or wood: item 29. The beneficiary is mainly whoever rules your stove.
Sources (3 references)

Home kitchen ventilation, cooking fuels, and lung cancer risk in a prospective cohort of never smoking women in Shanghai, China. International Journal of Cancer, 136(3), 632-638. https://doi.org/10.1002/ijc.29020

If hot flashes and night sweats around menopause disrupt your life, get evaluated for hormone therapy — don't tough it out, don't self-medicate, and don't use it to prevent heart disease

Grade AValue: highMetric: mortalityMoney: lowTime: mediumWillpower: noneBenefit: large

For menopausal hot flashes and night sweats, hormone therapy cuts hot-flash frequency by about 75% versus placebo. The price: slightly more breast cancer, clots, and stroke — about 8 extra cases each per 10,000 women per year. Starting at 50–59 showed no rise in total mortality. It is not for preventing heart disease or dementia.

Cost
One visit to gynecology or a menopause clinic. The doctor takes a history, checks for contraindications, and prescribes if appropriate. Follow-up as instructed. The hard part is letting go of the fear that "hormones mean cancer" — and not buying them for anti-aging.
Benefit
Cochrane pooled 24 randomized trials, 3,329 people, oral hormones versus placebo. Hormone users had about 75% fewer weekly hot flashes than placebo (95% CI 64.3–82.3, the confidence range). Severity also fell sharply (OR 0.13, 0.07–0.23). Placebo users' hot flashes fell about 57.7% too — anything claiming to treat hot flashes must beat placebo to count. Risks come from the US WHI randomized trial: 16,608 women aged 50–79 with a uterus, estrogen plus progestin, average 5.2 years. Coronary disease about 29% higher (HR 1.29, 1.02–1.63). Invasive breast cancer about 26% (HR 1.26, 1.00–1.59). Stroke about 41% (HR 1.41, 1.07–1.85). Pulmonary embolism about 2.13 times (HR 2.13, 1.39–3.25). In absolute terms per 10,000 women per year: 7 more coronary events, 8 more strokes, 8 more pulmonary embolisms, 8 more invasive breast cancers — and 6 fewer colorectal cancers, 5 fewer hip fractures. Women without a uterus on estrogen alone, followed 13 years, ran about 21% lower breast cancer (HR 0.79, 0.65–0.97). Both trials pooled over 18 years: total mortality unchanged (HR 0.99, 0.94–1.03). By starting age, the 50–59 group ran about 31% lower mortality during treatment years (HR 0.69, 0.51–0.94); 60–69 was 1.04 (0.87–1.25) and 70–79 1.13 (0.94–1.36), both nonsignificant. At 18 years, the 50–59 group was 0.89 (0.79–1.01), also nonsignificant. Cochrane's 2017 review, women 50–59 only: the one clear increase was clots on combined therapy, absolute risk under 1/500. Women over 65 on combined therapy: dementia rose from 9 to 11–30 cases per thousand over 4 years. The US Preventive Services Task Force 2022 recommends against hormones for chronic-disease prevention (grade D) — no net benefit.
Note
Contested: WHI women averaged 63 on one fixed oral regimen. Today most users are around 50, just menopausal, treating symptoms — not the trial population. The lower mortality in the 50–59 subgroup emerged only in age-split analysis and faded by 18 years, so hormones can't be called life-extending. Cochrane also notes the trials lack power for women within 10 years of menopause. Generally unsuited: those with prior breast cancer, prior clots, high cardiovascular risk, or marked obesity — the doctor decides. Women with a uterus on estrogen alone raise endometrial cancer, hence added progestin; only the uterus-removed may take estrogen alone. Hormones also reduce fractures, but are usually considered only when other osteoporosis drugs don't suit. For osteoporosis, see Section 1, items 39 (bone density) and 40 (medicate it). Benefit sized "large" on the 75% hot-flash reduction — a symptom endpoint, not mortality. The beneficiary is mainly you, and your mother and partner too.
Sources (6 references)

(2002). Risks and benefits of estrogen plus progestin in healthy postmenopausal women: principal results from the Women's Health Initiative randomized controlled trial. 44

If you already want a dog, count the daily walk toward your step total — don't get one for longevity

Grade BValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: highTime: highWillpower: yesBenefit: large

Dog owners run about a quarter lower mortality on average over the same period, and lower still after heart attack or stroke. But after adjustment, the big UK and Norwegian studies see no difference — and cats show no association either. So don't get a dog for longevity; if you wanted one anyway, count the walks as your walking.

Cost
A dog is permanent spending — food, vaccines, deworming, vet visits, registration — until it dies of old age. Daily walking time, and someone to cover travel. The hard part is doing it every day; a dog isn't something you can stop wanting. No official Chinese statistics on dog costs, so no numbers here.
Benefit
Pooling 10 cohort studies, about 3.84 million people, average 10.1 years. Dog owners: mortality about 24% lower (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.67–0.86, the confidence range). Cardiovascular death about 31% lower (RR 0.69, 0.67–0.71). Among coronary patients, dog owners ran about 65% lower (RR 0.35, 0.17–0.69). The authors state this pool applied no adjustment. Sweden's registry of ~3.43 million adjusted for income, marriage, and more. Dog ownership for people living alone: mortality about 33% lower (HR 0.67, 0.65–0.69); living with others, about 11% (HR 0.89, 0.87–0.91). Post-heart-attack in Sweden: living alone with a dog, about 33% lower (HR 0.67, 0.61–0.75); with partner or child, about 15% (HR 0.85, 0.80–0.90). Post-ischemic-stroke: about 27% (HR 0.73, 0.66–0.80) and 12% (HR 0.88, 0.83–0.93). The other side: 6 UK survey waves, 59,352 people, average 11.5 years. Fully adjusted, dog ownership showed no association with death (HR 1.03, 0.98–1.09) or cardiovascular death (HR 1.07, 0.96–1.18). A Norwegian study, median 18.5 years: dog owners' mortality essentially identical (HR 1.00, 0.91–1.09), and their activity wasn't higher either. The Swedish twin registry, 34,202 people with lifestyle data, failed to reproduce the lower cardiovascular and mortality risk. An Australian study, 15,735 people over 4 years: dog owners about 23% lower mortality (OR 0.77, 0.59–0.99), partly explained by activity. Cats, birds, and fish show no mortality association. The American Heart Association's 2013 statement rated pet ownership, especially dogs, "may be reasonable" for reducing cardiovascular risk — the weakest tier — and explicitly opposed adopting, rescuing, or buying pets primarily for cardiovascular risk reduction.
Note
Contested. All record-keeping, no assignment — so "get a dog to live longer" can't be derived. Would-be dog owners are healthier and more active to begin with; the ill and disabled are less likely to keep dogs — uncleanable confounds. The pooled 24% adjusted for nothing; in the studies that could ask about lifestyle, the difference vanished. In another Swedish study, dog owners actually started blood-pressure and lipid medication slightly more often — so even if their mortality is truly lower, it isn't via lower blood pressure or lipids. The one actionable bit: if you have or want a dog, count the daily walk toward item 11 (7,000–8,000 steps). Leashes, vaccines, and liability for bites: Section 8, item 30 (leash your dog). How elders should hold the leash to avoid falls: Section 17, item 10. The benefit is mechanically sized "large" on the unadjusted 24%. The beneficiary is mainly you.
Sources (8 references)

3. Don't waste energy

25 entries

This section counts only energy and time. Four things: the attention you have each day, how fast you react, how often you err, and how long it takes to come back after an interruption. All numbers are directly measured — from experiments, or from tracking groups of people (cohort studies). They are not converted into life-years or mortality. Most entries here are Grade B; that's the state of the field, not a sign the advice is wrong. Item 19 — expectations when dealing with police, doctors, and counter clerks — cites regulations, not experiments, so it's Grade C. Items 15 (treat pessimistic thoughts as a symptom) and 22 (treat "others demand I be perfect" as a symptom) cite mortality and suicide-risk numbers, a different metric from the rest of this section, so they aren't ranked alongside the others. Entries in this section are grouped by theme, with item numbers in parentheses. Attention at work: turn off non-essential notifications (item 1), batch messages a few times daily (item 5), block even seconds-long interruptions (item 6), do one thing at a time (item 7), earplugs in open offices (item 12), don't endlessly extend weekly work hours (item 13). Sleep and late nights: fix your wake time (item 2), sleep 7–8 hours nightly (item 3), no caffeine after 2 p.m. (item 4), no screens the hour before bed (item 8), sleep when it's time (item 9), no big decisions late at night (item 10), nap 10 minutes when the afternoon slump hits (item 11). Thought loops: switch to a hands-on task when rumination starts (item 14), treat pessimistic thoughts as a symptom (item 15), halve your estimate when you feel you embarrassed yourself (item 21), treat "others demand I be perfect" as a symptom (item 22). Anger and low mood: leave the scene first when angry (item 17), first steps when mood sinks (item 18), don't vent anger by smashing things (item 23), write your worries down for several days running (item 24). People and social media: learn to refuse requests you don't want (item 16), treat police and doctors as people working by rules (item 19), limit apps full of peers' updates (item 20). Bodily pain: take ibuprofen-type painkillers for menstrual cramps (item 25).

1

Turn off non-essential notifications, and keep the phone out of sight while working

Grade BValue: highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

One phone buzz — even unseen, untouched — drops your attention-task performance. By about as much as actually taking the call or texting. Worse: with the phone just sitting on the desk, resisting the urge to look still shrinks your usable headroom. The more phone-dependent you are, the bigger the drop.

Cost
Free. A few minutes changing settings; almost no willpower.
Benefit
Merely receiving one notification, without looking or touching, measurably worsens attention-task performance — by an amount comparable to actually calling or texting. This was in a lab, with students. Two further experiments: even when people successfully resisted checking, having their own phone beside them reduced available cognitive capacity. The most phone-dependent dropped most.
Note
These are single lab tasks. Nobody has measured the cumulative effect of doing this daily for years. If your job truly requires being reachable, whitelist a handful of contacts.
Sources (2 references)
Stothart, Mitchum & Yehnert (2015). The attentional cost of receiving a cell phone notification. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance. https://doi.org/10.1037/xhp0000100；Ward, Duke, Gneezy & Bos (2017). Brain Drain: The Mere Presence of One's Own Smartphone Reduces Available Cognitive Capacity. Journal of the Association for Consumer Research. https://doi.org/10.1086/691462
2

Fix your wake time — weekends included

Grade BValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

The most irregular fifth of sleepers run a body clock about 2.5 hours later than the most regular fifth — like living in permanent jet lag. The more regular the schedule, the better the grades.

Cost
Free. Sleeping in less on weekends takes a little willpower.
Benefit
61 students logged 30 days. The most irregular fifth's circadian clock ran about 2.5 hours later than the most regular fifth's — specifically, melatonin onset at 00:08 versus 21:32. Their sleepiest window also fell about 1.8 hours later. The more regular the schedule, the better the academic performance (correlation r = 0.37).
Note
One study, few people, no control group. The researchers inferred the clock differences come mostly from differing daily light exposure — so fix your wake time together with morning daylight, or it won't work. For recovering after the occasional late night, see Section 2, item 38 (catch up the next night): go to bed early that night, not sleep till noon next day.
Sources (1 references)
Phillips et al. (2017). Irregular sleep/wake patterns are associated with poorer academic performance and delayed circadian and sleep/wake timing. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-03171-4
3

Sleep 7–8 hours a night — don't treat 6 as enough

Grade AValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: highWillpower: someBenefit: large

Two weeks of 6-hour nights drags your mental performance down to the level of two full sleepless days and nights. The trouble is you can't feel it: self-rated sleepiness rises for a few days and then plateaus — 6-hour sleepers rate themselves as sleepy as 4-hour sleepers. So "6 hours is enough for me" is itself a symptom of sleep deprivation.

Cost
Free. Reserve 1–2 more hours for sleep daily. Going to bed earlier takes some willpower.
Benefit
48 healthy adults aged 21–38 slept only 6 hours nightly for 14 consecutive days. Their cognitive performance declined cumulatively to the equivalent of 2 full nights without sleep. Yet self-rated sleepiness rose only in the first days and then barely moved. The 6-hour and 4-hour groups rated themselves equally sleepy. This was a randomized controlled trial (RCT). Separately, short total deprivation (under 48 hours) affects simple-attention lapses with effect size g = −0.776 and reasoning accuracy g = −0.125. That part pools 70 studies.
Note
"I don't feel sleepy" is not evidence of enough sleep. Long-term 6-hour sleepers have merely habituated subjectively; performance hasn't kept up. The pooled part concerns whole nights skipped. Chronic short sleep rests on one RCT. Sleep duration versus death risk is a separate account — Section 2, item 13 (about 7 hours): by mortality, the 7-hour band is lowest.
Sources (2 references)
Van Dongen, Maislin, Mullington & Dinges (2003). The cumulative cost of additional wakefulness. Sleep. https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/26.2.117；Lim & Dinges (2010). A meta-analysis of the impact of short-term sleep deprivation on cognitive variables. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018883
4

No caffeine after 2 p.m.

Grade AValue: highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

A large coffee (400 mg) 6 hours before bed costs over an hour of instrument-measured sleep that night. Yet your own sleep diary shows no difference. An ordinary cup (107 mg) needs to be finished 8.8+ hours before bed to leave sleep alone. If you sleep at eleven, 2 p.m. is the line.

Cost
Free. Afternoon-coffee drinkers need some willpower to skip it.
Benefit
400 mg of caffeine 6 hours before bed cut instrument-measured total sleep by 1.1–1.2 hours versus placebo. A placebo is a caffeine-free control drink. Yet participants' own sleep diaries showed no difference — they couldn't tell. A pooled analysis (meta-analysis): caffeine cuts total sleep by 45 minutes on average. Sleep efficiency — the share of time in bed actually asleep — falls 7%. One cup (107 mg) must be finished more than 8.8 hours before bed to avoid affecting sleep.
Note
The Drake study comes from one lab, and 400 mg is on the high side — two or three coffees. Slow caffeine metabolizers need an earlier cutoff. What skipping caffeine buys is sleep duration, stacking with item 3 (7–8 hours).
Sources (2 references)
Drake, Roehrs, Shambroom & Roth (2013). Caffeine effects on sleep taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before going to bed. Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5664/jcsm.3170；Gardiner et al. (2023). The effect of caffeine on subsequent sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep Medicine Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smrv.2023.101764
5

Batch email and messages into a few fixed times a day

Grade BValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

The same people compared two weeks. The week email was limited to 3 checks a day, day-to-day stress was clearly lower — with the same number of emails sent and received. Unrestricted, people checked 15.5 times a day on average.

Cost
Free. Takes some time to tell colleagues how often you reply. Resisting the constant inbox check takes some willpower.
Benefit
124 adults, two weeks of self-comparison (within-subject). The week with email limited to 3 daily checks showed clearly lower daily stress than the unlimited week (effect size Cohen's d = 0.37). Emails received and sent didn't differ between weeks. Unrestricted at the start, people checked email 15.5 times daily on average.
Note
One study, small-to-medium effect, measuring stress — not output. Instant messaging hasn't been studied directly; this is extrapolation.
Sources (1 references)
Kushlev & Dunn (2015). Checking email less frequently reduces stress. Computers in Human Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2014.11.005
6

When doing work that needs continuous thought, block even seconds-long interruptions

Grade BValue: very highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: large

An interruption averaging 2.8 seconds doubles the error rate on what follows. 4.4 seconds triples it. Field tracking also found the interrupted task takes 25 minutes on average to return to, with two other tasks inserted along the way. Interrupted people work faster — with higher stress, frustration, and effort.

Cost
Free. Close the door, put on headphones, or hang a do-not-disturb sign.
Benefit
Interruptions averaging 2.8 seconds double the step-error rate on sequential tasks; 4.4-second ones triple it. Lab work. A separate field study observed 24 office knowledge workers: they switched work topics every 11 minutes on average; 57% of topics were interrupted; returning to an interrupted topic took 25 minutes 26 seconds on average, with 2.26 other tasks interleaved. A 48-person experiment: interrupted people finished faster but reported more stress, frustration, time pressure, and effort.
Note
The field study split interruptions in two: people coming to you, and things you open yourself. Closing the door blocks only the first kind. The second kind needs item 1 (turn off notifications) and item 5 (batching) alongside.
Sources (3 references)
Altmann, Trafton & Hambrick (2014). Momentary interruptions can derail the train of thought. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0030986；Mark, Gonzalez & Harris (2005). No task left behind? Examining the nature of fragmented work. CHI 2005. https://doi.org/10.1145/1054972.1055017；Mark, Gudith & Klocke (2008). The cost of interrupted work: More speed and stress. CHI 2008. https://doi.org/10.1145/1357054.1357072

Do one thing at a time — don't answer messages mid-meeting

Grade BValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Every task switch slows reactions and invites errors. Heavy multi-screeners haven't trained up an ability to do several things at once — they actually perform worse on task-switching tests.

Cost
Free. Not answering messages in meetings takes some willpower.
Benefit
After task switches, reactions are measurably slower and more error-prone — from a review of many studies. Another lab study used students: heavy media multitaskers are more easily dragged off by irrelevant stimuli and irrelevant memories, and perform worse on task-switching tests.
Note
How much switching costs varies hugely by task; no single number offered. Ophir's is a same-time-point comparison — it can't separate "multitasking worsens attention" from "worse attention seeks multitasking."
Sources (2 references)
Monsell (2003). Task switching. Trends in Cognitive Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1364-6613(03)00028-7；Ophir, Nass & Wagner (2009). Cognitive control in media multitaskers. PNAS. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0903620106
8

No glowing screens the hour before bed — paper books or e-ink if you must read

Grade BValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: yesBenefit: medium

Reading a glowing screen before bed delays falling asleep by about 10 minutes versus paper, suppresses melatonin by 55%, and pushes the next day's body clock back over 1.5 hours — sleepier mornings, longer to fully wake.

Cost
Free. Putting the phone down an hour before bed fights inertia daily — willpower.
Benefit
A lab crossover trial — the same people under both conditions. Reading a light-emitting e-reader before bed meant falling asleep about 10 minutes slower than paper (25.7 vs 15.8 minutes). Evening melatonin suppressed 55%. The next day's circadian phase delayed by over 1.5 hours — melatonin onset at 22:31 versus 21:01. Next morning: sleepier, and taking longer to become fully alert.
Note
Small sample, tightly controlled lab conditions. At everyday phone brightness and durations the effect may be smaller. Whether night mode helps wasn't tested here.
Sources (1 references)
Chang, Aeschbach, Duffy & Czeisler (2015). Evening use of light-emitting eReaders negatively affects sleep, circadian timing, and next-morning alertness. PNAS. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1418490112
9

Sleep when it's time — don't lose nights to games, short videos, or pornography

Grade BValue: highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: yesBenefit: large

In 2025 Chinese people slept 6.97 hours a night on average, falling asleep at 0:10. People using phones or tablets before bed run over double the risk of insufficient sleep and 2.7 times the daytime sleepiness. Even a device merely present — unused — in the bedroom shows similar numbers. So the easy fix: the phone doesn't enter the bedroom.

Cost
Free. The hard part is the long fight against "one more episode." Keeping the phone out of the bedroom is the cheapest way.
Benefit
In 2025, average night sleep was 6.97 hours with sleep onset at 0:10 (Chinese Sleep Research Society). Portable-device users before bed: about 2.17 times the odds of insufficient sleep (OR 2.17). Poor sleep quality about 1.46 times (OR 1.46). Daytime sleepiness about 2.72 times (OR 2.72). A device merely present in the bedroom, unused, showed similar numbers — about 1.79, 1.53, 2.27 (OR 1.79/1.53/2.27). That part pools 20 cross-sectional surveys, 125,198 children and adolescents. Another cross-sectional survey: among 844 adults aged 18–94, phone use after lights-out meant slower sleep onset, lower sleep efficiency, and more daytime fatigue.
Note
Contested. The cost of late nights themselves is item 3 (7–8 hours). Whether pornography affects ordinary people's energy and cognition has no reliable evidence settling causation. One pooled analysis holds that "pornography problems" stem mostly from the mismatch between a person's beliefs and their own behavior, not the content itself. Another pooled 280 men and found viewing duration unrelated to erectile function with a partner. This entry targets only its theft of sleep hours. On the 6.97-hour and 0:10 figures: the Sleep Research Society's site hadn't posted the release (checked 2026-09); the Fujian health commission's reprint of the Health News report is the source of record.
Sources (5 references)
Carter et al. (2016). Association Between Portable Screen-Based Media Device Access or Use and Sleep Outcomes. JAMA Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapediatrics.2016.2341；Exelmans & Van den Bulck (2016). Bedtime mobile phone use and sleep in adults. (2018). Pornography Problems Due to Moral Incongruence: An Integrative Model with a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Archives of Sexual Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10508-018-1248-x (one side of the note's dispute); Prause N, Pfaus J (2015). Viewing Sexual Stimuli Associated with Greater Sexual Responsiveness, Not Erectile Dysfunction. Sexual Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1002/sm2.58 (the other side)
10

No big decisions or important messages late at night

Grade BValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: small

Well-rested people quickly learn to avoid high-risk options. After two sleepless nights, they keep picking the high-risk ones — more so with age. Nobody has measured what a few short hours does, but move important decisions to after you've slept.

Cost
Free. Just postponing things until after sleep.
Benefit
34 healthy people did the Iowa Gambling Task — a risk-decision experiment — after 49.5 hours awake. Rested, they quickly learned to avoid high-risk options. Sleep-deprived, they chose them more often. Older participants were affected more. One experiment, one study.
Note
The study covers the extreme of two full nights awake. What staying up till 2 a.m. does to ordinary people wasn't directly measured. The "no messages" half is author experience (Grade C) — it can wait until tomorrow.
Sources (1 references)
Killgore, Balkin & Wesensten (2006). Impaired decision making following 49 h of sleep deprivation. Journal of Sleep Research. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2869.2006.00487.x
11

Nap 10 minutes when the afternoon slump hits — not half an hour

Grade BValue: highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

A 10-minute nap revives you on the spot, and the effect lasts two and a half hours. 5 minutes does essentially nothing. 20 minutes takes half an hour to kick in. 30 minutes wakes you into a fog that performs worse than no nap at all.

Cost
Free. 10 minutes, plus somewhere to lie or lean.
Benefit
After a short night, a 10-minute nap immediately improved sleepiness, fatigue, energy, and cognitive performance, with part of the benefit persisting past 155 minutes. 5 minutes: almost no benefit. 20 minutes: benefits appear only after 35 minutes. 30 minutes: an initial stretch of sleep inertia — performance worse than no nap at first, improving only later.
Note
One lab study, healthy young subjects. If you can't fall asleep, don't force it. Whether lying still with eyes closed for 10 minutes helps has no research support. Napping past an hour links to higher mortality and coronary risk — Section 2, item 37 (naps under half an hour).
Sources (1 references)
Brooks & Lack (2006). A brief afternoon nap following nocturnal sleep restriction: Which nap duration is most recuperative? Sleep. https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/29.6.831
12

In open-plan offices, use earplugs or book a quiet room for memory work

Grade BValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: small

Background noise rising from 39 to 51 decibels means fewer words remembered, more fatigue, and less desire to work. On breaks, a nature film with sound restores energy better than continuing to sit in office noise.

Cost
Earplugs, a few dozen yuan. Booking a quiet room takes a little arranging.
Benefit
Students worked in a simulated open-plan office. Raising background noise from 39 to 51 dB (LAeq) meant fewer recalled words, higher self-rated fatigue, and lower motivation. A break watching a nature film with sound restored energy ratings better than river sounds alone or continued office noise.
Note
One lab study. The most damaging part of the noise is intelligible speech. White-noise headphones help with that, but this study didn't test them.
Sources (1 references)
Jahncke, Hygge, Halin, Green & Dimberg (2011). Open-plan office noise: Cognitive performance and restoration. Journal of Environmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvp.2011.07.002
13

Don't keep piling on weekly hours: past roughly 49, each extra hour yields less and less

Grade BValue: highMetric: timeMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

WWI British munitions-factory records show output tracking hours one-for-one up to 49 hours a week. Beyond 49, each extra hour buys less and less. At 70 hours a week, output was nearly identical to 56 — those extra 14 hours were wasted.

Cost
Possibly less overtime pay, and possibly a conversation with your boss.
Benefit
WWI British munitions workers' output records: below 49 weekly hours, output proportional to hours. Past 49, output growth slows. Peak at about 63 hours. 70-hour weeks produced almost exactly what 56-hour weeks did — 14 hours for nothing.
Note
The data are century-old factory work — physical, mostly female workers. Where the threshold sits for knowledge work may differ; the author says other jobs could sit higher or lower. What's solid is the direction: past some point, extra hours add almost no output. The specific 49 is not.
Sources (1 references)
Pencavel (2015). The Productivity of Working Hours. The Economic Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/ecoj.12166
14

When you catch yourself replaying the same bad event, switch to a hands-on task

Grade BValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Replaying the same bad event doesn't produce answers. It deepens depression, nails negative thoughts in place, makes problems less solvable and action less likely, and drains the people willing to listen. Catch yourself circling, go do something with your hands.

Cost
Free. The hard part is noticing you're replaying it (it's called rumination) — noticing itself takes practice.
Benefit
A review of many studies: rumination — replaying the same bad event — deepens depression. It reinforces negative thinking and weakens problem-solving. It obstructs actual action and exhausts supportive listeners. It correlates with anxiety, binge eating, alcohol misuse, and self-harm.
Note
The review gives direction, not numbers. "Switch tasks" is the author's practice. What the literature supports is one sentence: diverting attention beats circling in place. Which task to switch to has never been compared.
Sources (1 references)
Nolen-Hoeksema, Wisco & Lyubomirsky (2008). Rethinking Rumination. Perspectives on Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-6924.2008.00088.x
15

Treat "things will definitely get worse" as a symptom, not a fact

Grade BValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

In a 20-year twin study, each step up in pessimism added about 13% to mortality over the period, and about 20% to cardiovascular death. In the other direction, optimism scores bought no matching benefit. So the thing to treat is pessimism, not "insufficient positivity."

Cost
Free. The hard part is seeing the thought as a symptom rather than a fact.
Benefit
2,978 Australian twins over 50, average 20 years of follow-up, 1,068 deaths. Each standard deviation up on the pessimism scale: about 13% higher mortality (hazard ratio 1.134), 95% CI 1.065–1.207, P=8.85×10⁻⁵. Cardiovascular death about 20% higher (1.196, 1.045–1.368, P=0.0093). No link to cancer death. Optimism scores showed no clear association with mortality either.
Note
Contested. Observation only, no assignment. One might say "illness came first and caused the pessimism"; the authors counter that cancer deaths would then correlate too — they didn't. Still, unmeasured factors can't be excluded. Optimism wasn't protective, so don't force "positive thinking." What to do is stop treating pessimistic forecasts as accurate predictions of the future.
Sources (1 references)
Whitfield JB, Zhu G, Landers JG, Martin NG (2020). Pessimism is associated with greater all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, but optimism is not protective. Scientific Reports, 10, 12609. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-69388-y
16

Cut draining relationships; learn to refuse requests you don't want

Grade CValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: yesBenefit: medium

One draining person costs you more than one supportive person gains you — more consistently, too. So subtract before you add.

Cost
Free. Short-term social friction, possibly some relationships lost. Saying no takes real willpower.
Benefit
A survey of 120 widowed women aged 60–89: distressing interactions correlated with psychological well-being more consistently — and more strongly — than pleasant ones. On that result, one draining person's damage exceeds one supportive person's benefit.
Note
A special population, one-shot questionnaire, no direction of causation. It measured well-being, not energy; placing it in this section is the author's inference. What counts as "draining" has no objective standard — your own judgment is the only one.
Sources (1 references)
Rook (1984). The negative side of social interaction: Impact on psychological well-being. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.46.5.1097
17

When angry, leave the scene first — treat the other party as weather, not as an enemy

Grade BValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Reinterpreting what just happened, or stepping into the other person's shoes, genuinely lowers the emotion — the second one works better. Suppressing the display does nothing. And people who punish an offender keep replaying the episode longer afterward; those who don't retaliate move on faster. People overestimate in advance how good revenge will feel.

Cost
Free. In the moment: bite back the retort, walk away, decide later whether to deal with it. Takes a little practice.
Benefit
Pooling 306 experimental comparisons (meta-analysis): reappraisal — reframing what happened — has effect size d = 0.36 on emotion. Perspective-taking, d = 0.45. Distraction, d = 0.27. Suppressing the feeling: ineffective (d = −0.04). Three further experiments: those who punished an offender ruminated about them longer afterward; those who didn't "turned the page" faster. People overestimate the satisfaction revenge will bring.
Note
The pooled part measures emotional intensity, not energy, with small-to-medium effects. The revenge part is one set of experiments — hence B. The "empty boat" is Zhuangzi's parable: an empty boat drifts into yours and you don't get angry; a boat with someone in it, you do — though the collision is the same. That's analogy, not evidence. If there's real damage, take the legal routes of Sections 8 and 9 — far cheaper than blowing up on the spot.
Sources (2 references)
Webb TL, Miles E, Sheeran P (2012). Dealing with feeling: A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of strategies derived from the process model of emotion regulation. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0027600；Carlsmith KM, Wilson TD, Gilbert DT (2008). The paradoxical consequences of revenge. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0012165
18

When mood sinks, do the highest-value basics first: move, get sunlight, sleep on schedule, talk to someone, call 12356

Grade AValue: highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: mediumWillpower: someBenefit: large

For depression, walking and jogging work best, more intensity better — details in Section 22, item 6 (walk or run when mood is low). Light therapy is strong for seasonal depression and works for non-seasonal too. Online self-help CBT courses work; with guidance they work better at heavier symptom levels. When it feels unbearable, call 12356 first.

Cost
Free or nearly. Brisk walks, jogs, or strength training several times weekly. Daylight by day. A fixed schedule. One phone call when things feel unbearable.
Benefit
A network meta-analysis pooled 218 randomized trials, 14,170 people, against active control groups (people doing some other activity). Versus them, walking or jogging for depression: effect size g = −0.62 (95% CI −0.80 to −0.45). Yoga −0.55, strength training −0.49. Higher intensity, better effect. Pooled light-therapy studies: seasonal depression effect size 0.84 (0.60 to 1.08); non-seasonal 0.53 (0.18 to 0.89). Another analysis pooled individual patient data across studies of internet cognitive behavioral therapy (online self-help courses). Both guided and unguided beat controls. At moderate-severe levels (PHQ-9 above 9), guided was better. 12356 is the national psychological-assistance hotline, open no fewer than 18 hours daily.
Note
These are adjuncts for mild-to-moderate depression. Moderate-severe, or with suicidal thoughts, means medical care — call 12356 first (Section 1, item 25). The exercise trials are mostly small, and can't blind who's exercising the way drug trials can. The light studies run only to 2003 and are small. "Sleep on schedule" and "talk to someone" are author experience without separate citations. Don't turn "move" into a demand on a depressed person — ten minutes of walking counts.
Sources (4 references)
Noetel M et al. (2024). Effect of exercise for depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. BMJ. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2023-075847；Golden RN et al. (2005). The efficacy of light therapy in the treatment of mood disorders: a review and meta-analysis of the evidence. American Journal of Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.162.4.656；Karyotaki E et al. (2021).
