19

Treat police, doctors, and counter clerks as people working by rules, not as roles: paperwork and deadlines move things, not emotion

Grade CValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: small

Police, doctors, and clerks are people working to job rules, hemmed in by paperwork, deadlines, and oversight. Whether they're pleasant has almost nothing to do with whether your matter gets done, or in how many days. So collect receipts, note deadlines, appeal through channels — don't try to argue them into agreeing with you.

Cost
Free. What changes is your expectations and the order of your moves. The first time, you must resist the urge to "argue them into agreement."
Benefit
Swap how you deal with institutions: from "begging, fuming, retelling the grievance" to "collect documents, note deadlines, appeal through channels." What you save is repeated communication and rumination time. This is a one-time mental adjustment, not daily savings. What's checkable are the deadlines themselves, all written in regulations. Public-order (administrative) cases: 30 days from acceptance, extendable by 30 with approval from the next-level public security organ. Where a complainant exists and the case isn't filed, the non-filing notice must be delivered within 3 days; the complainant may request review within 7 days, decided within 30 days; if dissatisfied, 7 more days to petition one level up for re-examination.
Note
Why C: "many people treat the person behind the window as a role rather than a worker" is a judgment with no literature to cite. What can be cited is the rules half: deadlines, paperwork, and remedy channels are all in plain text. The numbers here all come from the two ministry regulations also cited in Section 8, item 39 (what happens after you report to police). Following procedure won't fix a bad attitude or guarantee success — it fixes your expectations and your first move. Bank tellers and government windows are the same: their actions are logged, reviewed, and audited. So keep receipts, ask for written confirmation, complain through channels — don't guess at "will they cheat me." Lawful priorities are published: emergency departments triage by severity, not arrival order (Section 24, item 7). To thank a doctor who saved you, use thank-you letters and satisfaction surveys — Section 24, item 11. Wanting to "send something so they try harder" toward law-enforcement is bribery, expressly an aggravating factor — Section 8, item 40. When you meet obvious differential treatment, complain; don't treat it as an unwritten rule to imitate.
Sources (2 references)
公安部 (2020). 公安机关办理刑事案件程序规定（公安部令第 159 号修正后，第一百七十一、一百七十八、一百七十九条）. http://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2020/content_5549884.htm；公安部 (2013/2019 修正). 公安机关办理行政案件程序规定（公安部令第 125 号、第 149 号）. http://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2013/content_2321117.htm
20

Don't make "how others are doing" your daily reading: cap or kill the apps that feed you peers' updates

Grade AValue: highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: yesBenefit: large

People who habitually compare upward online tend toward worse mood and lower self-esteem. Deactivating Facebook for four weeks slightly raised well-being — and slightly cut current-affairs knowledge. People limiting three social platforms to 10 minutes daily saw loneliness and depression drop in three weeks.

Cost
Free. Setting app limits or deactivating takes minutes. The hard part is not reopening them — a long fight against inertia.
Benefit
A pooled analysis (meta-analysis): 54 independent samples, 94 effect sizes, N = 36,583, three-level random-effects model. Online upward social comparison correlated with psychological maladjustment at r = 0.330 on average (95% CI 0.289–0.370, the confidence range). By outcome: social-evaluative negative emotions like fear of being looked down on 0.438; anxiety 0.382; depression 0.306; lower well-being 0.268; lower self-esteem 0.263. Age, culture, and collection year didn't change the strength. Longitudinal studies showed no stronger results than cross-sectional ones. A randomized controlled trial with 2,743 US Facebook users: 61% would accept deactivation for under 102 US dollars. Randomized to 4 weeks off versus control. Deactivation freed 60 minutes daily for the average subject. Subjective well-being index rose 0.09 SD — life satisfaction 0.12, anxiety 0.10, depression 0.09, happiness 0.08 — all surviving multiple-comparison correction. The authors offer a benchmark: positive-psychology interventions move well-being about +0.34 SD and depression about −0.23 SD. So this effect is about 25%–40% of a standard psychological intervention. The cost in the same window: current-affairs knowledge down 0.19 SD, political polarization down 0.16 SD. After the experiment, the deactivation group still used Facebook 12 minutes/day less than control (0.31 SD, a 23% reduction). Another RCT: 143 undergraduates randomized to cap Facebook, Instagram, and Snapchat at 10 minutes per platform daily versus use as usual. Three weeks in, the capped group's loneliness and depression fell clearly. Both groups' anxiety and fear of missing out were lower than baseline.
Note
The "correlation" half only says two things co-occur — it can't be read as cause; the authors themselves call for more longitudinal work. The randomized half does license causal claims, but the subjects were US Facebook users before the 2018 midterms; carrying it to Chinese platforms is a stretch. Hunt's is 143 undergraduates, and it's the only one. Effect sizes are all modest — don't expect deleting apps to solve mood problems. What to block is the "see how others are doing" class of use; staying in touch with family and friends, looking things up, and job hunting don't count. If you truly can't resist, start by killing push notifications, "people you may know," and the recommendation feed. Total screen-time accounts: Section 4, items 15–16 (hard caps on short video; no scrolling news). What to do when mood sinks: item 18 here. Buying back a sense of identity: Section 6, item 23. Spending more to "move up a notch": Section 6, item 24.
Sources (4 references)
Lei Y, Hu S, Sun Y, Zheng L (2026). "Looking up" linked to feeling down: a meta-analysis of online upward social comparison and psychological maladjustment. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1825169；Allcott H, Braghieri L, Eichmeyer S, Gentzkow M (2020). The Welfare Effects of Social Media. American Economic Review, 110(3), 629–676. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20190658；Allcott H, Braghieri L, Eichmeyer S, Gentzkow M (2019). The Welfare Effects of Social Media. NBER Working Paper No. 25514 (the specific figures here are verified word-for-word against this version; the published article's abstract omits them). https://www.nber.org/papers/w25514；Hunt MG, Marx R, Lipson C, Young J (2018). No More FOMO: Limiting Social Media Decreases Loneliness and Depression. Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 37(10), 751–768. https://doi.org/10.1521/jscp.2018.37.10.751
21

When you feel "everyone saw me embarrass myself," halve that estimate

Grade BValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: small

Walk into a room wearing an embarrassing T-shirt, and you'll think nearly half the room can identify who's on it; fewer than a quarter can. Wearing a shirt you think looks good, you'll overestimate sixfold. After conversations, people likewise underestimate how much the other person liked them. So when "everyone will remember my blunder" hits — halve it, and it's still too high.

Cost
Free. Just one extra question when nervous: did they really see it?
Benefit
Experiment 1: participants wore a Barry Manilow T-shirt into a room of others. Wearers estimated 46% of onlookers could correctly name the person on the shirt; actual accuracy was 23% — the estimate exactly double. Subtracting actual from estimated per session: an average overestimate of 23 percentage points (95% CI 9–38, the confidence range); dropping the two sessions with only 2–3 onlookers: 27 points (11–43). Experiment 2: participants chose a T-shirt they considered flattering. Average estimate 48%; actual accuracy 8% — sixfold. Another research program, three settings: stranger dyads, first-year roommates, adult workshops. People systematically underestimated how much conversation partners liked them and enjoyed the conversation — the authors call it the "liking gap." It appeared across conversation lengths and persisted between roommates for months.
Note
Why B: all small lab and campus studies, scenarios of T-shirts and stranger chats. Carrying them to "colleagues gossiping" or "misspeaking in a meeting" has no direct evidence. The numbers show the direction and rough multiplier of overestimation — not coefficients to apply. Others' opinions aren't all irrelevant. Where you're genuinely evaluated — interviews, defenses, appraisals, checkup reports — the evaluation is real; prepare for it. What deserves the discount is the everyday "everyone is watching me" feeling; the target there is your own estimation bias.
Sources (2 references)
Gilovich T, Medvec VH, Savitsky K (2000). The spotlight effect in social judgment: An egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 211–222. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.78.2.211；Boothby EJ, Cooney G, Sandstrom GM, Clark MS (2018). The Liking Gap in Conversations: Do People Like Us More Than We Think? Psychological Science, 29(11), 1742–1756. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797618783714
22

Treat "others demand I be perfect" as a symptom, not a fact

Grade BValue: averageMetric: mortalityMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: small

People who constantly feel "everyone around me demands perfection, and falling short means rejection" are more prone to suicidal ideation. "I demand perfection of myself" relates to suicidal ideation far more weakly — about a third as much. After subtracting pre-existing thoughts, the first feeling still tracks later increases in ideation, though modestly.

Cost
Free. The hard part is treating the thought as something to manage rather than an accurate measurement of others' actual demands.
Benefit
A pooled analysis (meta-analysis): 45 studies, N = 11,747, undergraduates through psychiatric patients, random-effects model. Weighted average correlations with suicidal ideation: perfectionistic concerns r = .28 (95% CI .24–.32, the confidence range; 42 studies, 7,936 people). Perfectionistic concerns is an umbrella: socially prescribed perfectionism, concern over mistakes, doubts about actions, and the gap between standards and reality. Socially prescribed perfectionism alone: r = .28 (.25–.32; 30 studies, 3,640). Perfectionistic strivings r = .10 (.07–.13; 31 studies, 4,588) — an umbrella of self-oriented perfectionism and personal standards. Parental criticism r = .20 (.11–.29). Versus suicide attempts: perfectionistic concerns r = .12 (.07–.17; 15 studies, 5,275). Socially prescribed perfectionism r = .19 (.08–.29; 8 studies, 689). The longitudinal part: after subtracting baseline suicidal ideation, socially prescribed perfectionism still tracked ideation at follow-up, modestly. Self-oriented and other-oriented perfectionism showed no association.
Note
Why B: most included studies are one-shot questionnaires — no time order. The correlation is moderate (about .28), explaining only a few percent to a tenth of variance. What's measured is ideation and attempts, not deaths — hence "small" on the surrogate-endpoint rule. The authors themselves flag possible publication bias in the concerns-attempts set — publication bias meaning studies with unwelcome results going unpublished. Imputing the missing studies left the direction unchanged. High standards aren't the problem, and there's no need to lower yours. The difference is where the standard comes from, and whether falling short means "I, as a person, am finished." Like the pessimistic forecasts in item 15, it's treatable as a symptom. Suicidal thoughts: call 12356 and move lethal means away — Section 1, item 25. What to do when someone voices them: Section 8, item 15. Depression screening for children: Section 30, item 8.
Sources (1 references)
Smith MM, Sherry SB, Chen S, Saklofske DH, Mushquash C, Flett GL, Hewitt PL (2018). The perniciousness of perfectionism: A meta-analytic review of the perfectionism-suicide relationship. Journal of Personality, 86(3), 522–542. https://doi.org/10.1111/jopy.12333
23

When angry, don't vent by smashing things, hitting a bag, or going for a run — slow the body down first

Grade AValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Punching a bag, smashing things, going for a run — arousing forms of "release" — don't lower anger overall. Calming methods like slow breathing, mindfulness, and meditation clearly cut anger and the urge to lash out.

Cost
Free. In the heat, do a few minutes of something that slows your heartbeat: breathe slowly, sit down, be still. The hard part is that venting is exactly what you crave.
Benefit
A pooled analysis of 154 studies, 184 samples, 10,189 people. Calming activities — deep breathing, mindfulness, meditation — reduced anger and aggression: effect size g = −0.63, 95% CI −0.82 to −0.43 (the confidence range). Stable across sex, race, age, and culture. Arousing activities — punching bags, jogging, cycling — did nothing overall: g = −0.02, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.09. The authors' conclusion: venting rage and going for a run are not working ways to cool it.
Note
What's measured is anger and aggression, not energy; the "time" metric is the author's classification: one less fight is one less mess to clean up. For in-the-moment tools, see Section 22, item 8 (cyclic sighing) and item 17 here (leave the scene). Running isn't useless: long-term it helps low mood — Section 22, item 6 (walk or run when mood is low). It's just not an in-the-moment anger cooler. Don't drive, message, or decide while furious. If someone is hitting you, leave and call the police — then the problem isn't your emotions: Section 8, item 43 (domestic violence).
Sources (1 references)
Kjærvik SL, Bushman BJ (2024). A meta-analytic review of anger management activities that increase or decrease arousal: What fuels or douses rage? Clinical Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpr.2024.102414
24

With something weighing on you, writing your thoughts and feelings down for several days can help — but don't expect it to cure

Grade BValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: small

Writing down bad events shows a small average benefit — very small. The pooled conclusions also disagree; two pools found no effect. It costs nearly nothing, so try it. With serious mood problems, don't substitute it for a doctor.

Cost
Free. The typical study protocol: 3–4 sessions of 15–20 minutes, writing about something distressing — your deepest thoughts and feelings.
Benefit
One analysis pooled 146 randomized studies (meta-analysis). People wrote or spoke about personally important matters. The average effect was positive and significant but tiny: effect size r = .075. Another pool admitted only RCTs: 30 trials combined, no significant effect on either physical or psychological health. Sixteen randomized trials in cancer patients and survivors: psychological, physical, and quality-of-life outcomes all nonsignificant — the psychological one g = 0.04, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.14 (the confidence range).
Note
Contested. For: the 146-study pool, positive but tiny. Against: two RCT-only pools finding nothing significant. The "how often, how long" in the cost row follows the original experimental design, as stated in Mogk's abstract. It's nearly free, quick, and doable alone — usable when you'd rather not talk or have no one to talk to. It measures neither energy nor time saved; the "time" metric is the author's classification. If writing makes you feel worse, stop and call 12356 — Section 1, item 25.
Sources (3 references)
Frattaroli J (2006). Experimental disclosure and its moderators: a meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.132.6.823；Mogk C, Otte S, Reinhold-Hurley B, Kröner-Herwig B (2006). Health effects of expressive writing on stressful or traumatic experiences - a meta-analysis. Psycho-Social Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2736499/；Zachariae R, O'Toole MS (2015). The effect of expressive writing intervention on psychological and physical health outcomes in cancer patients--a systematic review and meta-analysis. Psycho-Oncology. https://doi.org/10.1002/pon.3802
25

Take ibuprofen-type painkillers for menstrual cramps instead of toughing it out; if pain disrupts work or school, or three months of medication doesn't hold it, get a gynecology workup

Grade AValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

For menstrual cramps, ibuprofen-type drugs raise the share with clear pain relief from under 20% to about half — better than acetaminophen, at the price of somewhat more side effects. If pain disrupts work or school, if deep pain during sex, or if three months of medication doesn't control it, get checked for endometriosis. That disease takes 6.7 years on average to diagnose.

Cost
A box of ibuprofen runs a dozen-odd yuan, taken only on the painful days. If gynecology is needed, registration and an ultrasound cost some money and half a day.
Benefit
A Cochrane review pooled 80 randomized trials, 5,820 women with primary dysmenorrhea — cramps with no other identifiable cause. Versus placebo, NSAIDs relieved pain better (OR 4.37, 95% CI 3.76–5.09, the confidence range). In absolute terms: 18% of placebo takers got moderate-or-better relief versus 45%–53% on NSAIDs. The price: somewhat more side effects (OR 1.29, 1.11–1.51) — 10% on placebo versus 11%–14% on NSAIDs, mostly gastrointestinal (OR 1.58) and nervous-system reactions (OR 2.74). Versus acetaminophen, NSAIDs were also better (OR 1.89, 1.05–3.43), though from only 3 trials. Which NSAID is best: no difference found. The UK NICE guideline (updated 2024) lists situations suggesting endometriosis: chronic pelvic pain; dysmenorrhea affecting daily activities and quality of life; deep pain during or after sex. Also painful bowel movements during periods, blood in urine or painful urination during periods, and infertility with these symptoms. Girls 17 and under are included. The guideline suggests a trial of acetaminophen or NSAIDs first — say, 3 months. If relief is insufficient, proceed to further investigation. Normal gynecological exam and ultrasound don't rule it out. A study across 16 hospitals in 10 countries surveyed 1,418 women undergoing laparoscopy: from symptom onset to surgical diagnosis of endometriosis took 6.7 years on average, mostly lost in primary care. Diagnosed women averaged 10.8 fewer working hours weekly — mostly presenteeism, on the job but less productive. A Dutch online survey of 32,748 women aged 15–45: 13.8% had taken sick leave for menstruation, averaging 1.3 days yearly; 80.7% were at work but less productive during periods — equivalent to 8.9 lost days yearly.
Note
Over 60, prior GI bleeding, or on anticoagulants or hormones: ask a doctor first. Details in Section 34, item 3 (ibuprofen-type painkillers). The US ibuprofen label states it can cause serious allergic reactions, more likely in aspirin-sensitive people, with asthma attacks among the presentations — asthmatics should ask a doctor first too. If pregnancy is possible, ask first; after 20 weeks don't self-medicate — Section 34, item 5. Those who can't take NSAIDs can use acetaminophen, daily cap in Section 34, item 1. Menstrual cramps mean medication only on period days; the 15-days-a-month ceiling in Section 34, item 9 concerns headaches, and cramp days are far from it. Grade A because the pain-relief numbers come from many randomized trials; the authors rated most comparisons low quality — poorly reported methods, 59% industry-funded. The "medium" benefit is judgment: the review measured pain, not sick days. In the Dutch survey, menstrual losses ran about 10 days a year — hours per week. The endometriosis cohort had already reached laparoscopy; it doesn't mean most cramp sufferers have it. The beneficiary is mainly you.
Sources (5 references)
Marjoribanks J, Ayeleke RO, Farquhar C, Proctor M (2015). Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for dysmenorrhoea. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (7):CD001751. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD001751.pub3；National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2017, updated 2024). Endometriosis: diagnosis and management (NG73), recommendations 1.3.1, 1.4.2, 1.4.3, 1.5.4. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng73/chapter/Recommendations；Nnoaham KE, Hummelshoj L, Webster P, et al.; World Endometriosis Research Foundation Global Study of Women's Health consortium (2011). Impact of endometriosis on quality of life and work productivity: a multicenter study across ten countries. Fertility and Sterility, 96(2):366-373.e8. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fertnstert.2011.05.090；Schoep ME, Adang EMM, Maas JWM, De Bie B, Aarts JWM, Nieboer TE (2019). Productivity loss due to menstruation-related symptoms: a nationwide cross-sectional survey among 32 748 women. BMJ Open, 9(6):e026186. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-026186；Haleon (2026). Advil (ibuprofen capsule, liquid filled), OTC drug label: Warnings. DailyMed. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=1f…

4. Don't waste time

18 entries

This section counts only time: hours saved per day, week, or year, or the improvement in the share of things finished on schedule. Time is not converted into lifespan or money here. Where money is involved, only the method is given, not a verdict. Most entries rest on single studies or time-use survey aggregates, so grades run mostly B and C.

1

Write "I intend to do X" as "at what time, where, and in response to what"

Grade AValue: very highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Rewrite "I'll do this thing" as "Tuesday 8 a.m., at the desk, I start with the introduction." Across 94 tests pooled, people who write it that way hit their goals clearly more often — a medium-to-large effect. All that changed is the phrasing of one sentence: free, effortless.

Cost
Free. One to two minutes per item, writing one "if… then…" sentence — say, "Tuesday 8 a.m., sitting down at the desk, I start with the introduction."
Benefit
Pooling 94 independent tests, people who first wrote intentions as "if… then…" achieved their goals more often. The format is called implementation intentions in psychology. Effect size d = 0.65, medium-to-large. It helps at three points: getting started, holding firm when interrupted, and withdrawing from doomed efforts.
Note
This works only for things you genuinely want. If the goal itself isn't yours, no number of sentences helps. Also, these studies mostly recruited students for health habits; transferring them to work settings isn't guaranteed.
Sources (1 references)
Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(06)38002-1
2

Write down your exit conditions before starting

Grade BValue: highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

Before starting, write one sentence: "If by date X I haven't hit indicator Y, I stop." Pooled studies confirm this format genuinely helps people withdraw from doomed efforts. What you save is all the time you would otherwise keep pouring in.

Cost
Free. Five minutes at kickoff, writing "if metric X isn't met by date Y, I stop." The hard part is honoring it on the day — stopping in front of others stings a little.
Benefit
Pooling implementation-intention studies: pre-written "if… then…" plans also help people disengage from failing courses of action — the paper's phrase. The time saved is what you would otherwise keep investing.
Note
Set exit conditions at kickoff, while calm. Setting them later gets bent by costs already sunk. Judge only on future investment versus future return — item 3. Also, "willingness to withdraw" is one sub-finding in a pooled analysis; nobody has separately computed the hours it saves.
Sources (1 references)
Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(06)38002-1
3

When deciding whether to continue, count only future investment and future return — not what's already spent

Grade BValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Money and time already spent make you want to keep going. Across 98 data sets pooled, the tendency is robust. So to decide whether to continue, count only what more you'd put in and what you'd get back. What's already spent: leave it out.

Cost
Free. The hard part is accepting that the time already invested is gone and unrecoverable.
Benefit
Money, effort, and time already invested make people more likely to continue — the sunk-cost effect in psychology. Pooling 98 data sets confirms the tendency is stable. Avoiding it means you stop investing time just to "not waste" what's gone.
Note
The Arkes and Blumer theater experiment: Ohio University theater sold season tickets at random for the full $15, $2 off, or $7 off. In the first half-season, the full-price group attended 4.11 shows on average, the others 3.32 and 3.29. By the second half, the groups no longer differed. Roth et al. found the effect fades with time, and older people are less swayed.
Sources (2 references)
Arkes, H. R., & Blumer, C. (1985). The psychology of sunk cost. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 35, 124–140. https://doi.org/10.1016/0749-5978(85)90049-4；Roth, S., Robbert, T., & Straus, L. (2015). On the sunk-cost effect in economic decision-making: A meta-analytic review. Business Research, 8(1), 99–138. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40685-014-0014-8
4

Estimate durations from how long similar past tasks actually took, not from the plan

Grade BValue: very highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Students estimated 33.9 days to finish their theses; they took 55.5, and only 29.7% finished by their own estimate. Another group was asked to recall how long a similar past task took before estimating — on-time completion rose from 29.3% to 60.0%.

Cost
Free. A few minutes before estimating, checking how long the last similar thing actually took.
Benefit
Students predicted 33.9 days for their theses; actual was 55.5. Only 29.7% finished by their own estimate. The researchers had another group connect the task to past experience before estimating. On-time completion rose from the control's 29.3% to 60.0%. The optimism that shrinks estimates vanished in that group.
Note
Buehler used Canadian students only — one study, small numbers: 37 and about 40 per group. Estimating from historical data of similar projects is called reference-class forecasting; how engineers do it is in Flyvbjerg. Halkjelsvik's review notes underestimation is more common than overestimation, but the size varies widely by task and method.
Sources (3 references)
Buehler, R., Griffin, D., & Ross, M. (1994). Exploring the "planning fallacy": Why people underestimate their task completion times. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 67(3), 366–381. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.67.3.366；Flyvbjerg, B. (2006). From Nobel Prize to project management: Getting risks right. Project Management Journal, 37(3), 5–15. https://doi.org/10.1177/875697280603700302；Halkjelsvik, T., & Jørgensen, M. (2012). From origami to software development: A review of studies on judgment-based predictions of performance time. Psychological Bulletin, 138(2), 238–271. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0025996
5

Circulate an agenda before meetings; no agenda, no meeting — and stand if you can

Grade BValue: highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Meetings with pre-circulated agendas are likelier to feel useful to participants. In an experiment, seated meetings ran 34% longer than standing ones — with no difference in decision quality.

Cost
Free. The organizer spends 5–10 minutes writing an agenda. Standing meetings need participants' cooperation.
Benefit
Two surveys, 958 and 292 people: meetings with pre-circulated agendas were likelier to be perceived as effective, a statistically solid relationship. In another experiment, 55 groups met seated, 56 standing; seated meetings lasted 34% longer. Decision quality didn't differ.
Note
The standing experiment used 5-person lab groups. Long meetings and large conferences don't transfer. Leach measured perceived effectiveness, not output.
Sources (2 references)
Leach, D. J., Rogelberg, S. G., Warr, P. B., & Burnfield, J. L. (2009). Perceived meeting effectiveness: The role of design characteristics. Journal of Business and Psychology, 24(1), 65–76. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10869-009-9092-6；Bluedorn, A. C., Turban, D. B., & Love, M. S. (1999). The effects of stand-up and sit-down meeting formats on meeting outcomes. Journal of Applied Psychology, 84(2). https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.84.2.277
6

Cut meeting count; anything solvable asynchronously in text doesn't need a meeting

Grade BValue: highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

The more meetings in a day, the more drained you feel and the heavier your workload feels. Cut one meeting and you save its full length — no discount.

Cost
Free. Needs colleague and boss cooperation. The hard part: writing a clear paragraph takes more effort than opening your mouth.
Benefit
Two surveys of employees working 35+ hours weekly, 676 and 304 people. How much time meetings take doesn't have a fixed effect on attitudes and well-being; it depends on meeting quality and how interdependent the job is. A diary study across one week: more meetings per day meant more fatigue and higher perceived workload. Time saved equals exactly the length of the meetings you cut.
Note
Contested: Rogelberg 2006 found the meeting–well-being link isn't one-sided; in highly interdependent jobs, many meetings aren't bad per se. And no study has directly compared "switch to async text" against meetings — that step is the author's inference.
Sources (2 references)
Rogelberg, S. G., Leach, D. J., Warr, P. B., & Burnfield, J. L. (2006). "Not another meeting!" Are meeting time demands related to employee well-being? Journal of Applied Psychology, 91(1). https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.91.1.83；Luong, A., & Rogelberg, S. G. (2005). Meetings and more meetings: The relationship between meeting load and the daily well-being of employees. Group Dynamics: Theory, Research, and Practice, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1037/1089-2699.9.1.58
7

Break big tasks into subtasks before estimating and starting

Grade BValue: highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

People don't automatically unpack multi-part tasks when estimating. List the subtasks first and your estimate shrinks less. Once split, each small step is immediately startable — and procrastination loses its grip.

Cost
Free. The splitting itself takes 5–15 minutes.
Benefit
When estimating, people don't spontaneously split a multi-part task — literature review, discussion, references are really several tasks. Listing subtasks first reduces the underestimation error called the planning fallacy. Once split, each step becomes an action you can begin at once, and procrastination drops. The strongest predictors of procrastination in research include task aversiveness and the task being pushed later.
Note
How fine to split: each subtask should fit in one sitting; over-splitting wastes time itself. Also, Kruger and Evans was verified from the abstract for direction only — the specific percentages weren't checked against the full text.
Sources (2 references)
Kruger, J., & Evans, M. (2004). If you don't want to be late, enumerate: Unpacking reduces the planning fallacy. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 40(5), 586–598. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2003.11.001；Steel, P. (2007). The nature of procrastination: A meta-analytic and theoretical review of quintessential self-regulatory failure. Psychological Bulletin, 133(1). https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.133.1.65
8

Set your own date for things without external deadlines

Grade BValue: highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

With a deadline set by others, 80.6% of students finish in time. Only 38.7% finish within their own predicted time. When you finish is almost entirely set by the deadline, barely by your estimate. So for things without deadlines, set one — and honor it.

Cost
Free. The hard part is honoring it — a date you ignore on the day equals no date.
Benefit
Students with external deadlines: 80.6% finished in time. Those finishing within their own prediction: 38.7%. Completion tracks the deadline almost completely, correlation r = 0.82 — the closer to 1, the tighter the tracking. Own predictions: only a weak relationship.
Note
Tell others your self-set date and it approaches the externally-set kind. Note the research validates other-imposed deadlines; self-imposed ones — timeboxing, Pomodoro — haven't been directly tested. This is extrapolation.
Sources (1 references)
Buehler, R., Griffin, D., & Ross, M. (1994). Exploring the "planning fallacy": Why people underestimate their task completion times. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 67(3), 366–381. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.67.3.366
9

Treat procrastination as avoiding discomfort, not as insufficient effort

Grade AValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Procrastination has little to do with laziness or character. What best predicts it is how aversive the task feels, whether you believe you can do it, and how easily you're pulled away by the immediate. So the useful move is making the task less aversive and the first step smaller — not scolding yourself and charging anyway.

Cost
Free. What changes is the direction of judgment: first ask what about the task hurts, then act.
Benefit
A meta-analysis of 691 correlations found strong, stable links with procrastination for: task aversiveness, time until deadline, self-efficacy (believing you can), impulsivity, and conscientiousness with its facets — self-control, distractibility, organization, achievement motivation. Neuroticism, rebelliousness, and sensation-seeking showed only weak links. The author explains the pattern with temporal motivation theory: a task's present appeal shrinks fast as its reward recedes.
Note
Benefit is "medium" because these studies give direction only — no hours-saved measurement. The concrete moves are item 1 (write when-where-what), item 7 (split into subtasks), item 8 (set your own date). These are pooled correlations — no causation implied.
Sources (1 references)
Steel P (2007). The nature of procrastination: a meta-analytic and theoretical review of quintessential self-regulatory failure. Psychological Bulletin, 133(1), 65–94. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.133.1.65
10

Put what you need within reach and what you avoid far away — don't count on in-the-moment willpower

Grade BValue: highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Things a little farther away get taken a little less. The same snacks moved farther away get eaten clearly less — a medium effect. Fewer options on display, clearly fewer takers. None of this needs in-the-moment willpower; a few minutes of setup does it.

Cost
Free, a few minutes once. Phone to another room; book and computer open on the desk.
Benefit
A Cochrane review including 24 randomized trials. Placing food farther away reduced consumption: standardized mean difference −0.60 (95% CI −0.84 to −0.36, the confidence range; 12 studies, 1,098 people, low-certainty evidence) — a medium effect. Reducing available options cut selection of the food even more: SMD −1.13 (95% CI −1.90 to −0.37, 3 studies, 154 people, low-certainty). Regression showed: farther away and fewer alternatives, stronger the effect.
Note
Why B: all 24 included studies concerned food — none on alcohol or tobacco; 14 were lab studies, all from high-income countries. So "farther away, less touched" carried to phones and games is extrapolation, not direct trial. The one directly measured piece — phone out of sight — is Section 3, item 1 (turn off notifications; phone out of sight while working).
Sources (1 references)
Hollands GJ, Carter P, Anwer S, et al. (2019). Altering the availability or proximity of food, alcohol, and tobacco products to change their selection and consumption. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 9, CD012573. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD012573.pub3
11

To make yourself follow through, stake money — but first ask whether you'd accept the stake

Grade AValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: lowTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

To force yourself, you can take a reward for succeeding, or post a deposit returned only on success plus a bonus. Among people willing to do both, deposit-takers outperform by 13 percentage points. But only 13.7% accept deposits while 90% accept rewards — deposits work only for those who'll take them.

Cost
Deposit-style programs require putting up your own money, forfeited on failure. The trial staked $150.
Benefit
A US randomized trial of 2,538 people assigned employees and their family or friends to four incentive designs or usual care. Reward-type (about $800 for success) acceptance was 90.0%; deposit-type ($150 up front plus a $650 bonus), 13.7%. Six-month sustained abstinence: 9.4%–16.0% across the four designs versus 6.0% usual care. Reward-type 15.7%, deposit-type 10.2%. But among only the 13.7% willing to enter either, deposit-type beat reward-type by 13.2 percentage points at 6 months (95% CI 3.1 to 22.8, the confidence range).
Note
The trial measured quitting smoking; carrying it to theses and gym attendance is extrapolation — hence "medium." When choosing, first check whether you'd actually use the design. A method most people refuse doesn't help those people, however strong its effect. Pick the kind you'd accept; a small stake beats none. For quitting smoking itself, see Section 2, item 3 (cessation medication).
Sources (1 references)
Halpern SD, French B, Small DS, et al. (2015). Randomized trial of four financial-incentive programs for smoking cessation. New England Journal of Medicine, 372(22), 2108–2117. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1414293
12

Count new habits in months, not "21 days"

Grade BValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: yesBenefit: medium

"21 days to build a habit" has no basis. A 12-week tracking study found an action becomes automatic in as little as 18 days or as long as 254. Still feeling effortful after a few weeks is normal. Missing one day doesn't reset progress.

Cost
Free. What it takes: repeating the same action in the same context daily, for months.
Benefit
96 volunteers each picked an eating, drinking, or activity behavior to perform daily in a fixed context ("after breakfast") for 12 weeks, self-rating automaticity daily. 82 provided analyzable data; the model fit 62. Days to reach 95% of each person's automaticity ceiling ranged from 18 to 254. Missing one performance opportunity had no material impact on habit formation.
Note
One study, 96 people, all simple actions (a piece of fruit after a meal). How long complex ones take — running thrice weekly, daily writing — hasn't been measured. So still struggling after two weeks isn't evidence of failure. To make repetition happen, bind the action to a fixed context — item 1 (write when-where-what).
Sources (1 references)
Lally P, van Jaarsveld CHM, Potts HWW, Wardle J (2010). How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology, 40(6), 998–1009. https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.674
13

If procrastination is disrupting your life, use self-help material backed by randomized trials — no therapist required

Grade AValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: mediumWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Procrastination severe enough to cause suffering is treatable. Ten weeks of cognitive-behavioral self-help, guided or unguided, clearly beats nothing. Guided versus unguided showed no difference — so working through it alone works too.

Cost
A self-help book costs a few dozen yuan; some are free. About ten weeks of investment, one chapter and one exercise weekly.
Benefit
150 people randomized to therapist-guided self-help, unguided self-help, or waitlist. After ten weeks, between-group effect sizes on the pure procrastination scale: guided d = 0.70 (95% CI 0.29–1.10, the confidence range), unguided d = 0.50 (0.10–0.90); on the irrational procrastination scale, 0.81 (0.40–1.22) and 0.69 (0.29–1.09). Clinically significant improvement: guided 31.3%–40.0%, unguided 24.0%–36.0%. No significant difference on any outcome.
Note
Swedish adults, Swedish-language materials; no ready-made Chinese equivalent — hence "medium." The ingredients are the usual: behavioral activation, behavioral experiments, stimulus control, psychoeducation on motivation and work methods. Stimulus control is item 10 (move what you avoid far away). If procrastination comes with clear low mood or anxiety, start with Section 3, item 18 (move, sunlight, sleep, talk, call 12356).
Sources (1 references)
Rozental A, Forsell E, Svensson A, Andersson G, Carlbring P (2015). Internet-based cognitive-behavior therapy for procrastination: A randomized controlled trial. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 83(4), 808–824. https://doi.org/10.1037/ccp0000023
14

Use your hourly rate to decide which chores to outsource

Grade BValue: highMetric: timeMoney: highTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Chinese people average 1 hour 17 minutes of housework daily; those who actually did housework that day, 1 hour 59. People who spend money to buy time are more satisfied with life. The same money spent buying time brings more in-the-moment happiness than buying things.

Cost
The outsourcing itself costs money, depending on the service. Plus one-time effort to compute your hourly rate.
Benefit
Chinese residents average 1 hour 17 minutes of daily housework; counting only those who did any, 1 hour 59 minutes. A 2024 survey covering 38,500 households, 107,000 people. Another study sampled 6,271 people across four countries: those spending money to buy time had higher life satisfaction. The researchers also ran real-life experiments: the same sum spent buying time brought higher momentary well-being than buying material goods.
Note
First compute the hourly rate: monthly after-tax income ÷ actual monthly work hours. Then price the chore's outsourcing. If the price is below your rate and you'll truly use the freed time for earning or rest, outsource. Rates and prices differ per person — do your own math. Also, Whillans measured happiness after buying time, not hours saved.
Sources (2 references)
Whillans, A. V., Dunn, E. W., Smeets, P., Bekkers, R., & Norton, M. I. (2017). Buying time promotes happiness. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1706541114；国家统计局 (2024). 第三次全国时间利用调查公报（第二号）. https://www.stats.gov.cn/sj/zxfb/202410/t20241031_1957216.html
15

Set hard caps on short video and aimless scrolling

Grade CValue: highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: yesBenefit: large

Chinese people average 5 hours 37 minutes online daily; those actually online that day, 6 hours 3. In 2018 the same measure showed 2 hours 42. This is the biggest number in this section. Cut one hour a day and you gain 365 hours a year.

Cost
Free. The action takes minutes: kill push, delete the app, or set a daily limit. The hard part is the hand discipline — not tapping open.
Benefit
Chinese residents average 5 hours 37 minutes online daily; those online that day, 6 hours 3 minutes. 92.9% used the internet that day. These are 2024 figures. In 2018 the same method showed only 2 hours 42 minutes — the biggest number in this section. Cutting one hour daily equals 365 hours a year. Per CNNIC, by June 2025 netizens averaged 30.6 hours online weekly, up 1.9 from six months before. Short-video users numbered 1.068 billion, 95.1% of netizens.
Note
Online time includes work, study, and social contact — not all waste. Grade C because no study has measured "how much is reclaimed after capping, and where it goes" — we hold only aggregate statistics. For the "seeing how others are doing" class specifically, a randomized trial measured reclaimed time and mood: Section 3, item 20.

No TV and no scrolling news; read what you need in scheduled batches

Grade CValue: highMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

Americans 15+ watch 2.6 hours of TV daily — half of all leisure. Chinese people average 1 hour 40 minutes; those 75–84 watch 3 hours 16. Switch to scheduled batch reading, and you reclaim the whole block.

Cost
Free. The hard part is breaking the reflex to open it — plus possibly missing some instant news.
Benefit
Americans 15+ watch 2.6 hours of TV daily out of 5.2 hours of leisure — half. 2025 figures. Chinese residents average 1 hour 40 minutes of TV daily; ages 75–84 watch 3 hours 16 minutes (2018 figures).

Only aggregate statistics in hand. No study has measured where the reclaimed time goes after cutting TV and news. "Batch reading" is author experience.

Spend once on learning keyboard shortcuts and automation for software you use daily

Grade BValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: noneTime: mediumWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Most people who've used Word for years still click toolbar icons. In grouped experiments, shortcuts beat menus and icons for speed. Learning is a one-time cost that pays back on every operation, every day. The longer you do the same kind of work, the more it returns.

Cost
Free. A one-time investment of hours to tens of hours. The hard part: it's slower than the mouse at first.
Benefit
The study examined 251 experienced Word users; most rarely used the faster shortcuts, working mainly from icon toolbars. Grouped experiments confirmed that among menus, icons, and shortcuts, shortcuts were fastest. Time saved accumulates with daily operation count. People doing the same work long-term gain most.
Note
Learn only operations you use ten-plus times daily; learning too broadly is its own waste. Note: the efficiency experiment had 6 participants, and the abstract gives no per-operation seconds saved.

When choosing where to live, put commute length first — shorten the one-way commute

Grade BValue: averageMetric: timeMoney: highTime: mediumWillpower: noneBenefit: large

The longer the commute, the worse people feel about their lives — and that loss is not compensated in salary or housing. Thirty minutes less one-way is 5 hours a week.

Cost
High. Possibly higher rent or a smaller home. Moving itself takes time.
Benefit
Chinese residents spend 50 minutes daily on transport on average; counting only those who traveled, 1 hour 2 minutes (2024). German panel data following the same people show longer commuters with stably lower subjective well-being, uncompensated by income or housing. A review across studies confirms commute time predicts commute dissatisfaction regardless of transport mode. Thirty minutes less one-way saves about 5 hours weekly.
Note
Contested: Chatterjee's review finds no stable relationship between commute length and overall life satisfaction — people largely trade the loss back via better jobs or housing. Note too that the transport statistics count all travel, not just commuting. And with off-peak hours, the same road runs shorter.

5. Don't waste money

46 entries

This section counts only money: what gets saved, how annual returns differ, what a sum returns on long average. None of it converts into lifespan or time. Investment entries only show how to run the numbers, using verified historical data only — none of it is investment advice. Entries in this section are grouped by theme, with item numbers in parentheses. Daily spending: turn off auto-renewal (item 1), re-shop your phone and broadband plans (item 4), decline electronics extended warranties (item 11), choose drugs that won volume-based procurement (item 12), drink boiled tap water (item 14), pay per gym visit (item 21), cooling-off period for big purchases (item 23), don't stockpile for the strikethrough price (item 24). Impulse spending and kids' spending: no lottery tickets (item 5), no tipping streamers (item 8), kids' recharges and tips can be reclaimed (item 9), anyone asking your child for a verification code is a scammer (item 10), count bracelets and designer toys at money spent (item 33), jewelry and jade only with a CMA report (item 34), randomized sales like blind boxes and card pulls (item 35). Online shopping and rights enforcement: written contracts for prepayment (item 22), know the platform rules when shopping online (item 29), things bought in livestreams that go wrong (item 30), ten times the price for unsafe food (item 31), check inspections and certifications before big purchases (item 32), buy prepackaged if you want to read the ingredient list (item 36). Tax, housing fund, insurance (social): annual tax reconciliation (item 2), housing fund withdrawable for rent and renovation (item 3), family sharing on medical insurance (item 13), personal pension account (item 20), if self-paying employee pension insurance, pay the lowest tier (item 46). Saving, borrowing, investing: walk away at "high returns" (item 6), convert loans to annualized rates (item 7), don't trade stocks frequently (item 15), never borrow to invest (item 16), broad index funds as the base (item 17), choose low-fee funds (item 18), don't bet everything on one place (item 19), emergency fund first (item 27), compare before prepaying the mortgage (item 28), sell losing stocks by rule (item 37), US stocks via QDII or Stock Connect (item 38), no crypto (item 45). Insurance: prefer pure protection insurance (item 25), buy enough third-party liability (item 26), insure only losses you can't absorb (item 39), term life for the earner first (item 40), cancel within the free-look period (item 41), tell deposits from insurance at the bank counter (item 42), no "surrender agents" (item 43), name a specific beneficiary (item 44).

1

Turn off all auto-renewal; renew manually at expiry

Grade CValue: highMetric: moneyMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

What you save is the subscriptions you stopped using long ago that still charge monthly. Going through the lists takes under 20 minutes. By regulation, merchants must conspicuously remind you before charging and give you an always-available, easy-to-find, easy-to-tap cancellation option.

Cost
Free. Go through the auto-debit lists in Alipay, WeChat, Apple, and Android — 10–20 minutes once. From then on, every renewal costs you one extra tap.
Benefit
What you save equals the sum of subscriptions you no longer use but still pay for — different for everyone, no standard number. Regulators require merchants to remind you conspicuously before renewal and to offer "simple, anytime cancellation," free of charge (China, effective 2021)
Note
For services you genuinely use constantly, annual billing usually beats monthly — keeping auto-renewal on is actually rational there. What to kill are the ones you've forgotten that keep charging.

Do the annual individual income tax reconciliation between March and June, and fill in every special deduction you qualify for

Grade AValue: highMetric: moneyMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

These people usually get money back: anyone who worked only part of the year, changed jobs mid-year, or never filled in deductions for children's education, mortgage, rent, or supporting the elderly. A dozen-odd minutes on your phone. If your annual comprehensive income is under 120,000 yuan, or the tax you'd owe is under 400 yuan, you may skip it.

Cost
Free. Done in the "Individual Income Tax" app in a dozen-odd minutes.
Benefit
Wages, labor remuneration, authorship royalties, and licensing fees are settled in one combined account: overpayments refunded, shortfalls paid. Two situations exempt you: annual comprehensive income under 120,000 yuan, or additional tax under 400 yuan — per the State Taxation Administration's 2023 announcement, valid through 2027-12-31. Conversely, refunds usually go to: those with income only part of the year, job changers mid-year, and those with unfilled deductions for children's education, mortgage, rent, elder support, and the like
Note
Those who owe must also file — skipping is illegal. There are seven special additional deductions: children's education, continuing education, serious-illness medical, home-loan interest, rent, elder support, and infant care under 3. Mortgage and rent are mutually exclusive — fill one, not both

Free. One trip to file the withdrawal.
Benefit
The amended regulations list nine withdrawal situations, including: paying rent, renovating your own home, and paying property fees on your own home. The fund center must decide within 3 days of accepting your application

Re-shop your mobile and broadband plans yearly; downgrade what you don't use; if the carrier won't switch you, complain

Grade AValue: averageMetric: moneyMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Your old plan is often a few dozen yuan more expensive than current ones. A few dozen a month is a few hundred a year thrown away. By regulation, carriers may not refuse your number portability without legitimate cause, may not drag their feet, and may not set up special tariffs just for porting customers. If they stall, complain.

Cost
Free. One bill check, a dozen-odd minutes. The hard part is holding firm against the retention script.
Benefit
MIIT rules state carriers may not "refuse, obstruct, or delay number-portability service without legitimate cause," may not "use interception, restriction, or other technical means to degrade service quality for ported users," and may not "set exclusive tariff or marketing schemes for porting users." Old plans often cost a few dozen yuan more than current ones — staying put wastes a few hundred yearly
Note
First check six months of actual data and minutes in the carrier's app, then pick a plan for that usage. If the agent says "downgrades need a store visit" or "you're in a contract term," demand the written basis. None produced? Call 12300 and complain

5

Don't buy lottery tickets

Grade AValue: highMetric: moneyMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

By regulation, lotto and numeric games must return at least 50% of sales as prizes; the Double Color Ball returns 51%. So every 1 yuan you put in returns 0.51 on long average — a steady 49% loss. In 2024, China sold 623.486 billion yuan of lottery; 161.031 billion went straight to public-welfare funds, outside the prize pool.

Cost
Free. Not buying is the saving.
Benefit
The Ministry of Finance sets minimum prize ratios by game type: lotto and numeric 50%, scratch cards 65%, sports betting 73%. The Double Color Ball allocates 51% of sales to prizes — of every 100 yuan sold, only 51 go to prizes. For you: every 1 yuan invested returns 0.51 on long average, losing 49%. 2024 national lottery sales were 623.486 billion yuan, of which 161.031 billion went to public-welfare funds, never returning to buyers (China, 2024)
Note
The long-run loss is built into the system — luck has nothing to do with it. Buy if you like, but only as 2-yuan entertainment, never as investing.

Walk away the moment you hear "high returns," "capital guaranteed," "steady gains"

Grade AValue: very highMetric: moneyMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: large

The regulator's own words: question anything above 6% returns, treat 8%+ as dangerous, and above 10% prepare to lose all principal. Legitimate wealth products are no longer allowed to promise principal or returns. Money lost to illegal fundraising is, by rule, your own loss — nobody backstops you.

Cost
Free. Just pause when the words appear.
Benefit
The then-banking-regulator chairman said it at the 2018 Lujiazui Forum: "question returns above 6%, above 8% is very dangerous, above 10% be prepared to lose all principal." The asset-management rules require institutions to "not promise principal protection or returns" and to "not advance funds in any form when redemption difficulties arise" — so no legitimate product promises safety anymore. Losses from illegal fundraising "are borne by the participants themselves"; when it blows up, no one compensates you (China, 2018, 2021)
Note
The 6/8/10 lines are a regulator's rules of thumb, not statute. The quote was about illegal fundraising — high-return products and investment firms. Not investment advice.

7

Skip credit-card minimum payments; no installments or consumer loans for spending. If you must borrow, convert everything to annualized rates before comparing

Grade CValue: averageMetric: moneyMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Minimum payment is a daily-interest loan running about 18% a year — and using it voids your grace period. Installments quoting "0.6% monthly fee" are about 13.8% annually, not 7.2% — because the principal shrinks monthly while the fee keeps charging on the original amount. To compare loan costs, look only at the annualized rate, never the daily rate or monthly fee.

Cost
Free. Keep enough cash to pay in full before the statement date. The hard part is resisting installments that spread out big purchases. When borrowing is unavoidable, spend a few minutes getting each loan's annualized rate.
Benefit
Credit-card overdraft rates used to have caps: a "daily rate of 0.05%" ceiling, floor at 0.7× that. 0.05% daily annualizes to 18.25% simple — interest not compounding into principal. Since 2021, pricing is negotiated between issuer and cardholder. Once you use the minimum payment, the unpaid principal accrues daily interest in full, and the grace period is voided. The central bank requires issuers to display the annualized rate prominently and "not display only the daily rate or daily payment amount." Since 2021, all lenders must show the annualized rate prominently in ads and contracts; daily and monthly rates may appear alongside but not more conspicuously. The annualized rate must include interest and all directly related fees. For amortizing loans, the money you actually use is what remains after each repayment. The PBOC's worked example: borrow 100,000 yuan over 12 months, paying 0.5% of the original principal monthly as installment fees, plus a 1,000-yuan service charge upfront. Simple interest: about 12.80% annualized. Compounded (IRR method): about 13.58%. By the nominal fee math you'd think you paid 0.5% × 12 + 1% = 7% — actually nearly double, because the principal shrinks monthly while fees keep charging on 100,000. Same arithmetic on a 12-installment card plan at 0.6% per period, no other fees: nominally 7.2% a year, but about 13.8% annualized — roughly 1.9× nominal; across 6–36 installments it's 1.8–2×. Loans from individuals or ordinary companies are private lending: rates exceeding 4× the one-year LPR at signing get no court support for the excess. The one-year LPR on 2026-08-20 was 3.0%, so 4× = 12%. Interest deducted upfront counts the actually-received amount as principal. This cap doesn't bind licensed banks and consumer-finance companies, nor seven classes of local financial organizations (small-loan, pawn, leasing, etc.) — so don't apply 12% to them; read the annualized rate on the contract (China, 2020, 2021)
Note
18.25% is 0.05% × 365 straight, no compounding — rolling monthly would be higher. Some banks discount; your statement's stated annualized rate governs. When truly short, borrow from cheaper legitimate channels rather than rolling minimum payments. Comparing loans: ask for the compounded (IRR) annualized rate; if they quote simple interest, regulation requires it be labeled "simple," and simple reads lower than compounded. The 13.8% and 1.8–2× figures are this book's own arithmetic per the PBOC method, shown in the verification record. For loan sharks, see Section 7, item 15 (no loan-shark borrowing).
Sources (5 references)
中国人民银行 (2020). 关于推进信用卡透支利率市场化改革的通知（银发〔2020〕327 号）. https://xining.pbc.gov.cn/zhengwugongkai/4081330/4406346/46…；中国人民银行 (2021). 中国人民银行公告〔2021〕第 3 号（第一、三、四条，附件《采用内部收益率法计算贷款年化利率示例》第三例）. https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/2021-03/31/content_559…；最高人民法院 (2020 年第二次修正). 关于审理民间借贷案件适用法律若干问题的规定（第一、二十五、二十六条）. http://gongbao.court.gov.cn/Details/94b6623974526df7d2430a3…（最高人民法院公报）；最高人民法院 (2020). 关于新民间借贷司法解释适用范围问题的批复（法释〔2020〕27 号）. https://www.court.gov.cn/fabu/xiangqing/285171.html；全国银行间同业拆借中心受中国人民银行授权 (2026). 2026 年 8 月 20 日贷款市场报价利率（LPR）公告. https://www.chinamoney.com.cn/chinese/rdgz/20260820/3399885…

No tipping streamers, no game top-ups, no impulse orders

Grade BValue: averageMetric: moneyMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Chinese gamers spend about 480 yuan per person per year on games — spent, essentially unrecoverable. The law lets only minors' un-consented spending be refunded; adults have no such provision. The cheapest defense is set up in advance: no password-free payment, limits, unbound payment methods.

Cost
Free. Three actions in minutes: disable password-free payment, set per-transaction and daily limits, remove bound payment methods. The hard part is not tapping in the moment.
Benefit
This is a large outlay. 2024 domestic gaming revenue: 325.783 billion yuan across 674 million users — about 480 yuan per head (dividing those two figures). Money spent is essentially unrecoverable. One exception: tips and top-ups by persons with limited civil capacity (here, minors) without guardian consent — "the people's court shall support" the guardian's demand for refund. Adult tips and top-ups have no such rule. Separately, minors may play online games only on Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays, and statutory holidays, 20:00–21:00 (China, 2020, 2021)
Note
Grade B because no one has directly measured "money saved by not tipping" — only industry aggregates. Disabling password-free payment and setting limits are practice-based, Grade C alone. The Civil Code articles 19 and 145 are quoted verbatim in item 9 (kids' top-ups and tips). Not investment advice.

If your child recharged or tipped from your phone, large spending by a child over eight can be reclaimed without parental ratification

Grade AValue: averageMetric: moneyMoney: noneTime: mediumWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Money spent by a child over eight, when the amount is clearly disproportionate to their age and intelligence, and the parent neither consented nor ratifies — that transaction is void and refundable. Under eight, children can't commit binding spending at all. A parent who stays silent is legally deemed to refuse ratification.

Cost
Free. It takes time to gather evidence and negotiate with the platform — which usually refuses first, refunds later. Failing that, litigation runs months minimum, with your own attorney fees. So assembling the file and going through the platform and 12315 is the cheaper route. The hard part: the child won't talk; you must ask patiently.
Benefit
Minors over eight have limited civil capacity: they may independently do only acts fitting their age and intelligence. Acts beyond that are valid only with the legal representative's consent or ratification — the parent's nod beforehand, or acceptance afterward. Under eight, a minor has no civil capacity; their affairs are transacted by the legal representative. Silence counts as refusal: a parent who never responds is deemed to reject the deal
Note
The key is proof: you must show it was the child operating the phone, not you. Useful materials: charges clustered during school or parents' work hours; device usage records; the child's chat and game records; the child's own statement. "Fitting age and intelligence" has no fixed money line — a few dozen yuan for a skin is not tens of thousands in tips. Prevention is cheaper: cap password-free payments, enable youth mode, never share the payment password. For your own impulse spending, see this section's "no streamer tips, no game top-ups, no impulse orders."

10

Teach your child one sentence: anyone who tells you to use your parents' phone or read out a verification code is a scammer

Grade BValue: highMetric: moneyMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: someBenefit: large

The six scam types differ, but the last step is always the same action: getting the child to transfer from a parent's phone or read out a verification code. So one sentence covers them all: whoever tells you to touch your parents' phone or read codes is a scammer. Add: "tell me first; I won't scold you." A child who dares speak the same day gives the money a chance of recovery.

Cost
Free. Walk the child through the six scam types below, and agree on one line: "tell me the day it happens — I won't scold you." Also cap password-free payments, enable youth mode, keep the payment password secret. The hard part is not erupting when it does happen.
Benefit
Quanzhou's anti-fraud center, with the city education bureau, dissected six scams aimed at teenagers. They differ in setup but share the final step: making the child use a parent's phone to transfer. Type 1: cheap private trades of game accounts and gear. One boy privately sent 260 yuan; the other side claimed "minors transferring violates rules — the account will be frozen"; he tapped the "verification link" on his father's phone and 30,000-odd yuan left the account. Type 2: "removing anti-addiction locks." Threats that "without paying to cancel, your parents will go to jail" — a child transferred 7,000 yuan from the mother's phone. The notice states anti-addiction locks are official and "there is no private unlock channel." Type 3: tip refunds. Scammers pose as "official customer service," claim minors' tips are refundable, then demand "gifts to a designated livestream room via the parent's Alipay to process the refund" — 73,000 yuan tipped from the mother's account, then blocked. "Anyone adding you to 'refund via gifting' is 100% a scam." Type 4: impersonating classmates or teachers. Hijacked accounts send voice messages with real names to borrow money; at term start, scammers join class group chats as the teacher posting "school fee 500 yuan," same avatar and nickname, with shills replying "paid." Type 5: celebrity-chasing. The child is pulled into a "star fan group, 888-yuan red envelope," asked to send 48.88 yuan to "verify," then threatened: "a minor broke rules — the platform will freeze 80,000 and your parents will go to jail." Total taken: 16,000 yuan. "Real police and lawyers never contact minors online for investigation, let alone ask for parents' phones." Type 6: secondhand platforms with cheap listings to lure people off-platform for private transfers. The same notice lists three red lines for kids themselves: never lend, sell, or rent bank or phone cards — cards used to launder money can constitute the crime of assisting information-network criminal activity, leaving a record that affects graduate exams and civil service; "phone-relay" part-time jobs are illegal; overseas "high-pay recruitment" can mean being controlled on arrival (national, October 2025)
Note
Grade B because the official material dissects scripts and cases, without incidence rates or prevention-effect statistics. Distinguish from item 9 (kids' top-ups): money the child spent on tips and recharges can be reclaimed under the Civil Code; money scammed away doesn't qualify — that's Section 8, item 2 (report and freeze). Recovery depends on whether the money is still in the account. The core threat — "you broke the rules, your parents will go to jail" — is itself the scam's signature; telling the child in advance beats interrogating after. Actually honor "tell me, no scolding": fear of scolding and concealment is the common thread that let these losses snowball. The adult versions, including AI face-swaps, are Section 8, items 3–4. For adults too: never do verification codes or face scans for anyone — Section 8, item 45.

Decline extended warranties on electronics

Grade BValue: highMetric: moneyMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Extended warranties sell for 10%–50% of the original price, at margins some 18 times ordinary goods — that markup is your overpayment. Main components like washer and fridge motors carry a state-mandated 3-year warranty anyway. For a very cheap warranty, divide its price by the cost of one repair; the result is the break-even failure probability.

Cost
Free. The price is paying out of pocket for a post-warranty repair — a low-probability event.
Benefit
Warranties typically price at 10%–50% of the item's original price. Industry estimates cited in the research put average gross margins at 50%–60%: of 100 yuan sold, 50–60 is profit — roughly 18× ordinary goods' margin. In 2003, warranties were 3%–4% of Best Buy's revenue but over half its profit (US, 2000s retail data). For warranties priced far below that band, run the math: warranty price ÷ one repair's cost = the failure probability needed to break even. Buy only if you estimate the odds of at least one failure during the coverage years exceed that. Example: a 25-yuan warranty against a hypothetical 300-yuan repair needs roughly 8%+ failure odds — the 300 is illustrative, not statistical. First subtract what the state already covers: the three-guarantee period runs from invoice date — washers and refrigerators 1 year whole-unit, 3 years main components (motors, timers, programmers, capacitors for washers; compressors, thermostats for fridges). A warranty overlapping the three-guarantee period buys what you already had (national, since 1995)
Note
The margin figure is an industry estimate the paper cites (Business Week 2004), not its own measurement. The math suits ordinary people who could absorb one repair bill. Anyone whose livelihood depends on one device with no backup should compute separately. Phone screen insurance deserves its own math: estimate your drop frequency, then check the premium. A very cheap warranty costs little either way — before buying, read three things: the start date (from purchase date means years overlapping the three-guarantee), who underwrites (merchant, brand, or third party), and whether call-out and parts cost extra. Check the manual and warranty card too: the brand's own promise may exceed the statutory minimum.
Sources (2 references)

Journal of Consumer Research 36(4):611-623. https://doi.org/10.1086/605298；国家经贸委等 (1995). 部分商品修理更换退货责任规定（国经贸〔1995〕458 号，第八条三包有效期自开具发票之日起计算；附件《实施三包的部分商品目录（第一批）》洗衣机、家用电冰箱整机 1 年、主要部件 3 年）. 国家市场监督管理总局行政规范性文件. https://www.samr.gov.cn/zw/zfxxgk/zc/xzgfxwj/art/2019/art_f…

Prefer generics that passed consistency evaluation and drugs selected in centralized procurement

Grade AValue: very highMetric: moneyMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: large

The second procurement batch averaged 53% price cuts, the deepest 93%. By April 2026, 11 batches covered 490 drugs. One extra question at the counter — "is there the procured generic?" — same ingredient, far less money.

Cost
Free. When the doctor prescribes or you buy, ask one question: "is there a procured generic (INN) version?"
Benefit
National centralized procurement's second batch averaged 53% off, max 93%. By April 2026: 11 batches, 490 drugs covered; 1,695 products passed or were deemed to pass consistency evaluation — roughly two-thirds of commonly used chemical drugs (China, official data 2020–2026)
Note
Contested: people say "consistency evaluation only compares ingredients, not efficacy." Half true. Passing means healthy volunteers take the drug, blood draws map the concentration curve, and that curve is compared against the originator's — within 80%–125% passes. Narrow-therapeutic-index drugs face stricter rules. Excipients — fillers and coatings beyond the active ingredient — may differ; the rules require only the same active ingredient, dosage form, dosing, and therapeutic action. So it is indeed not "give patients the drug for months and see if they get better." Patient outcomes are answered elsewhere: NHSA organized real-world studies across hospitals — by December 2024 covering 63 procured drugs, nearly 100 top hospitals, 300,000+ patients, all showing no difference from originators. Metformin, for instance: HbA1c on-target 83.4% generic vs 78.9% originator; fasting glucose on-target reversed — 83.8% vs 87.6%. Each side wins some. In January 2025, doctors publicly claimed procured drugs "don't lower blood pressure, anesthetics don't put people to sleep, laxatives don't work." Insurance and drug regulators investigated 7 Shanghai hospitals: most claims were hearsay and personal impression, and the named laxative wasn't yet in hospital use at the time. The same investigation acknowledged problem drugs do surface: of the first 9 batches' 1,600-plus selected products, 9 were disqualified over quality risks — 6 imported (3 originator), 3 domestic. Two things you can act on. First, if you want the originator, it's usually still prescribable: procurement covers 60%–80% of hospital purchasing, the rest is hospital discretion — originators aren't banned, only costlier out of pocket. Second, after a chronic-disease drug switch, don't judge by feel: track blood pressure, glucose, and HbA1c per Section 16, item 3 (one notebook for every reading). If it truly worsens, see the doctor and have them report the adverse reaction — don't self-stop.

One binding lets the money in your employee medical-insurance personal account pay for your spouse's, parents', and children's care and medicine. Without it, that money sits there for you alone.

Cost
Free. One family-sharing binding in your insurance region's app, or at a service office.
Benefit
The personal account can pay the out-of-pocket share of care at designated institutions for yourself and your spouse, parents, and children, plus out-of-pocket costs of drugs, devices, and consumables at designated pharmacies. Drink boiled tap water; skip the standing order of water-cooler jugs and bottled water

Grade CValue: highMetric: moneyMoney: noneTime: lowWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Beijing tap water works out to 0.005 yuan a liter. Cooler jugs at 20 yuan each run about 1 yuan a liter — 200-odd times dearer. A family drinking a jug a week spends just over 1,000 yuan a year; the same tap water costs under 5. Tap water has a mandatory national standard; boil and drink. When it smells or turns cloudy, boiling won't fix it — stop and report.

Cost
Buy a kettle. Each boil takes a little time plus a bit of gas or electricity.
Benefit
Beijing's first-tier water price is 5 yuan per cubic meter — 0.005 yuan per liter. Cooler jugs hold 18.9 liters; at 20 yuan, that's 1.06 per liter, about 210× tap water. A jug-a-week family: 52 jugs, 983 liters — about 1,040 yuan versus 4.9 yuan of tap water. Small bottles at 1 yuan per 500 ml are 2 yuan per liter, 400× tap. Drinking water follows the mandatory national standard GB 5749-2022, published 2022-03-15, effective 2023-04-01, administered by the National Disease Control Bureau (China, 2015 prices and the 2022 standard)
Note
The dispute: "compliant" is measured at the plant and pipe ends. Source or network failures can briefly break it. On 2025-07-16, the raw water entering Hangzhou Yuhang's Renhe plant smelled off; tap water in some neighborhoods stank. Official conclusion: algae decomposing under low oxygen produced sulfides. After the source switch, no total coliforms or E. coli were detected; all items met GB 5749-2022. Seven officials were held accountable, July water bills waived, filters replaced free. But fecal coliforms in the same source had been climbing for months: the Tiaoxi Yongsheng intake ran 10/L in April, 7,300/L in May, 16,000/L in June — against a GB 3838 Class-III limit of 10,000/L; Siling reservoir hit 28,000/L, Mantoushan 24,000/L the same month. Boiling kills microbes but removes neither odor compounds nor dissolved chemicals. If the water smells or turns yellow or cloudy: stop drinking, report to the utility and 12345, switch temporarily to bottled — don't hope extra minutes of boiling fix it. But this was a local, one-off accident, compensated per incident — still no case for permanently buying bottled. The "sewage pipe crossed" notice circulating online was a fabricated police bulletin; its author was criminally detained (see Section 9). The 20-yuan jug and 1-yuan bottle are assumptions for the arithmetic — redo with your city's prices. Jug water isn't the cleaner side either: Chongqing's regulator warns microbial risk grows with days after opening, and coolers need cleaning at least every 2–3 months. Old compounds with non-compliant secondary supply can filter — or buy water only for that case. Water prices vary; Beijing's number is for magnitude.
